title: What is this on my babys hand male 19 weeks 5 days
body: I noticed this perfect red line on my babys left hand under his pinky. It doesnt seem to bug him when I touch it and it hasn't lightened in color for the past few days since ive noticed it. Hes on no medicications, only takes a vitamin D drop everyday, fully breastfed, no health issues and was born full term and healthy.

real_comments.comment: Could be a cafe au lait macule, could be an early hemangioma. Just have the doc take a look at the next visit.

DG.comment: It's always a good idea to look very closely with a bright light to ensure there isn't a fine hair or thread wrapped around it. This is called a hair tourniquet and can be easy to miss.

SAG.comment: This is very common in infants due to them keeping their fists clenched. Moisture and lint get trapped in the skin folds, causing irritation. Keep it clean and dry, and it should clear up.

SAGII.comment: This looks like a normal palmar crease that has become irritated, which is very common in infants. Keep it clean and dry, especially after baths.

title: Getting a "second opinion" to calm my nerves I guess
body:
Hello, super sorry if this isn't anything to worry about but I just wanna be sure

So I (18F, 165cm, 48kg, white) had some health anxiety recently and got some blood tests done. Almost everything was within range except for my leukocytes. The results I was given said it should've been between 3.5 and 8.8, but it was at 9.4. I know it's probably nothing, but I tend to get nervous about stuff like that. Whenever I've previously gotten a blood test, it's been within the range I was told it should be, but it seems like it started to rise at some point this past year or so? I'm not currently sick and haven't been in the past few months I believe. I've been taking fluoxetine for the past 4 years, 40mg, and more recently I've been taking multivitamins and iron supplements because my blood count was down at a 95 (got it to 132 now). Is it the iron supplements raising by leukocyte count?

Sorry for wasting your time on this

real_comments.comment: No, the iron supplements are not increasing your white count. Your white count is still fine. Labs set their "normal" ranges by getting a bunch of healthy volunteers (often the people who work in the lab!) and setting the range so that 95% of those healthy volunteers would be in the normal range. That means that for each value, 5% of people may be out of range despite being perfectly healthy. Just having something out of range does NOT mean that there's anything wrong with you.

DG.comment: A white blood cell count of 9.4 is a very minor elevation and can even be considered within the normal range for many labs. Stress alone can cause it to fluctuate, so I wouldn't be concerned about that number by itself.

SAG.comment: A white blood cell count of 9.4 is still well within what is considered a normal physiologic range. This number on its own is not concerning.

SAGII.comment: A value of 9.4 is just barely outside that particular lab's reference range. All sorts of things, including stress, can cause a minor, temporary bump in your white count. On its own, this isn't a value that would typically cause any concern.

title: Middle ear infection, second round of antibiotics
body:
I’m 30F, no allergies or chronic illnesses. 

Prescribed AmoxiClav; pharmacy only had 20 not 21

 I’m in the third week of fighting a bad middle ear infection. I was on ear drops of Ciloxan before from my GP but it had limited effect. 

Now I’m on AmoxiClav from an ENT but the pharmacy had only 20/21 for me. Is this okay?

real_comments.comment:
Hi there, I would not worry too much about that. Is it prescribed twice a day or three times a day? Also do you mind sharing the dose?

Where I work we use a 875mg formulation twice a day, but 500mg three times a day may be the standard where you live.

Either way, it sounds like a 7 to 10 day course which is more than sufficient for a middle ear infection, if that’s your diagnosis.

DG.comment: For an ear infection, missing the very last dose of a 7 or 10-day course is very unlikely to cause a problem. Just finish the 20 pills you were given.
Makes sense to switch to an oral antibiotic like Amoxi-Clav. Topical drops often aren't sufficient for a true middle ear infection (otitis media).
If your symptoms (pain, pressure, hearing loss) haven't significantly improved by the time you finish the medication, you should let your ENT know.

SAG.comment: It's unlikely that missing the very last dose of a full course of antibiotics will make a difference. You can always call the pharmacy to see if they can get you the final pill, but finishing the 20 you have should be sufficient.
Missing the very last dose is unlikely to make a significant difference in your outcome. Just finish the 20 you were given.

One missed dose at the very end of a course is unlikely to make a difference in the outcome, especially if your symptoms have resolved. You could also call the pharmacy and see if they can provide the final dose now.

SAGII.comment: Being short one pill at the very end of the course is very unlikely to affect the outcome. Just make sure you take all 20 of the pills you were given.
Ciloxan drops are for outer ear infections and can't reach the middle ear where the infection is. It's good you were switched to an oral antibiotic.
AmoxiClav can be a bit rough on the stomach. Taking it with food can help, and you might also consider a probiotic to help prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea.

title: 34F on multiple meds starting ursodiol for gallbladder full of stones since 2017–18 — looking for experience/tips?
body:
Hi everyone,

I’m a **34-year-old female** who was diagnosed with **gallstones (entire gallbladder full)** back around **2017–2018** during an incidental ultrasound and have been managing it conservatively since. My doctor recently prescribed **ursodiol** to *try to shrink/dissolve* the stones.

Current meds I take regularly:  
• amitriptyline  
• bupropion XL  
• rosuvastatin  
• acyclovir  
• duloxetine DR  
• methocarbamol  
• gabapentin  
• **ursodiol**  
• lamotrigine

I understand ursodiol works by altering bile composition and can take months to show effects; some patient ratings are positive while others note side effects like GI upset, headaches, or dizziness.

Specifically curious about:  
• Typical *timeline* people saw change on imaging or symptoms  
• Experiences of stone *shrinkage or dissolution*  
• Side effects folks experienced — especially with other meds onboard  
• Any clinical monitoring you found useful

Thanks so much! ❤️

real_comments.comment: Takes up to a couple years for stones to go away but yes may take months before you notice symptomatic improvement. If you stop and don't change lifestyle, stones come back. Shouldn't really cause any interactions with other drugs.

DG.comment: The success rate of ursodiol really depends on the size and type of the stones. For a gallbladder full of stones, it's often less effective, and it can take many months to see any change. Surgery is usually the more definitive long-term solution if you become symptomatic.

SAG.comment: Ursodiol is most effective for small, cholesterol-based stones. For a gallbladder described as 'full,' the success rate can be lower, and it often takes 6-12 months to see any change on imaging.

SAGII.comment: Just be aware that ursodiol is most effective for small cholesterol stones and it's a very long process. With a gallbladder full of stones, success rates can be low and recurrence is common after you stop the medication.

title: Dissolvable stitches in a thigh scar
body: I am a 28 year old female, 163 cm, 65kg, I take Quinagolide and birth control, I don’t smoke or drink or take drugs, I recently had a deep tissue burns scar removed from my upper thigh. The surgeon used subcutaneous stitches and the resulting scar now appears bunched up and I’m looking for a way to reduce the way the scar appears. How long after a surgery should I begin massaging a scar? How long do subcutaneous dissolvable stitches take to dissolve? What should I massage my scar with? I also have a fresh scar on the back of my hand which has the stitches removed and is flat what should I do to help the scar heal?

real_comments.comment: This looks quite recent, since there is still surgical skin marker ink present. That will relax significantly with time. I would not be massaging it yet until cleared by your surgeon.

DG.comment: It's common for scars with deep stitches to appear bunched at first. You can usually start gentle massage once the incision is fully healed over, typically around 2-3 weeks. For both scars, using a silicone-based scar gel or sheet can help improve their final appearance.

SAG.comment: The bunched-up appearance is often intentional and allows the scar to flatten out over time. Depending on the material, dissolvable stitches can take anywhere from a few weeks to several months to fully absorb. You can typically start gentle massage once the incision is fully healed.

SAGII.comment: The 'bunching' is often intentional and helps the scar to heal flatter over time. It typically settles down over the first few months as the deep stitches dissolve.

title: Is it hemochromatosis? Or something else?
body:
Hi! I (20F) am very confused about what is happening in my body. I am waiting to hear back from my PCP, but in the meantime I would like to maybe get some answers. I’ll try to keep this as short as possible!

I thought that I had endometriosis because I have had very heavy periods, bad cramping, bloating, extreme fatigue, and some pain with sex. And this has been happening basically since I got my period. However, the fatigue got much worse over the last year and a half, and I’ve also lost my ability to focus. I’ve had depression and anxiety symptoms since then. I assumed that this was because I’ve been switching around birth controls because of my migraines, but I got an iron panel done on Wednesday, and now I’m just more confused. 

Story behind BC, I was on a Progesterone/Estrogen pill for a little over a year, started getting aura migraines, and was put on a progesterone only pill. That made me incredibly depressed, so I got off of BC completely for about 7 months. I got an IUD put in at the end of September, and I bled for about a month and a half after I got it in. I also had severe cramping with it in around the time I should have gotten my period. All this to say, I assumed my adverse effects were linked to hormone imbalance. I also assumed I was anemic in some way based on the heavy bleeding, because I was told I could take iron supplements in high school. I stopped them over a year ago, however. 

I got my ferritin levels checked two weeks ago, and instead of being low, they were super high! The exact level was 502. I thought it would just be because of my inflammation due to the cramping, etc. I then got that test redone, and I got my full iron panel done five days later. My ferritin was still high (411), but my iron level was perfect (126). My total iron binding capacity was low (217), and my unsaturated iron binding capacity was also low (91). My transferrin saturation was high (58%). All of these were done while fasting, hadn’t had alcohol in over a month, and wasn’t sick. All of my other tests looked great other than vitamin D (supplementing now, feeling good!). 

Everything I’ve read said that it most likely would be hemochromatosis, but I’m still a menstruating female and am super young for that diagnosis. Is there anything else that could be contributing to those iron levels?

real_comments.comment:
While theoretically possible, it is very unlikely that you have hereditary hemochromatosis (homozygous C282Y). It is *absolutely* impossible that you have clinically-relevant hemochromatosis causing your symptoms—the clinical complications of HH take decades to develop, and usually never develop in women.

Iron values (including ferritin and iron sat) are notorious for day-to-day variations, depending upon transient inflammation and even what you ate the day before. This is highlighted by the fact that your ferritin fluctuated by 100 points in 5 days. Consider rechecking again in a few weeks when you are feeling better, or maybe just let it go entirely.

DG.comment: Your transferrin saturation is quite high, which along with the elevated ferritin, does raise suspicion for an iron overload condition like hemochromatosis. It's less common in menstruating women your age, but certainly possible. The next step is usually genetic testing for the HFE gene.

SAG.comment: With a transferrin saturation that high, genetic testing for hemochromatosis would be a reasonable next step, even considering your age and sex.

SAGII.comment: A transferrin saturation that high is certainly concerning for iron overload. The next step would be genetic testing for hereditary hemochromatosis. While it's less common to present this early in menstruating females, it's the most common cause and needs to be ruled out.

title: Red Raised Painful Bump on 1.5 healed month old tattoo
body:
Age: 26M

Race: White

Height: 5'10"

Weight: 300 lbs

Preexisting conditions: asthma, gerd, primary hypertension

Smoker : no

Drinker: no

Current medications: none

On September 19th I got a tattoo while I was on vacation in Portland Oregon. The artist was reputable, used fresh needles, cleaned everything properly, etc.

About three weeks later I noticed a small angry bump on a spot that's not super heavily tattooed, the tattoo was basically healed and was actually very easy surprisingly as it's on my inner bicep.

At first I thought it was maybe a pimple so I didn't play with it because I didn't want to scar the new tattoo, but it's been hanging around for a few weeks. It's painful to touch, raised, firm, maybe 1/4" across, isn't warm. At one point I did try to pop it because I still believed it to be a pimple and the tiniest amount of liquid came out but nothing too much.

Wondering if anyone has any ideas what it may be?

real_comments.comment: I suspect localized folliculitis or furunculosis. It is likely to heal on its own. If the pain is increasing, redness is spreading, or you have systemic symptoms of an infection (fever, chills...), then seek care.

DG.comment: This could be a localized reaction to a component of the tattoo ink, like a granuloma. It can happen weeks to months after the tattoo has healed.

SAG.comment: This could be a foreign body granuloma, which is essentially a delayed inflammatory reaction to the ink pigment. I would avoid manipulating it any further.

SAGII.comment: This could be a small abscess or a deep folliculitis. Squeezing it can often make the inflammation worse and potentially drive any infection deeper.

title: What is it? 27M
body: Hello, I 27M have recently started getting pimples or warts on the base of my penis. I'm The worried about STI but the past few months I've only been with only one person 29F and we always use a condom. I do believe that one of the "bumps" is a cut from shaving. Please Help and thank you very much.

real_comments.comment: It’s possible this is folliculitis from shaving, but they also have the appearance of herpes vesicles. Any tingling sensations? If you see a doctor about it soon while they’re still open/crusting, they can swab and tell for sure whether it’s HSV

DG.comment: Bumps at the base of the penis are very commonly folliculitis, which is just inflamed hair follicles. This is especially common after shaving and can look like small pimples.

SAG.comment: It's very common to get inflamed hair follicles (folliculitis) from shaving in that area, which can look like pimples. This often resolves on its own if you stop shaving for a bit.

SAGII.comment: Given the location and history of shaving, folliculitis (inflamed hair follicles) is a strong possibility. The appearance could also be consistent with things like molluscum or HPV warts, which can be transmitted even with condom use.

title: Fever 3 days after surgical abortion
body:
I had a SA this past Saturday. Yesterday evening, I suddenly started having chills and felt very cold. When I got home from work 2 hours later, I checked my temperature and it was 100.7F. I quickly got under the blankets and my temperature rose to 103F. 

I stripped and took Tylenol and Advil. My temperature came down after 2 hours back to normal. I took Tylenol and then Advil once more after that. My last dose of medication was 7.5 hours ago. I sweated all night, my sheets are drenched. My temperature now is 97.8F.

My bleeding is not excessive. I'm not having any more pain other than some mild cramping here and there. No foul odor. 

I called my clinic and have a follow up appointment on Friday. I took a covid/flu/rsv test to be safe and it was negative.

Any thoughts on this? Its weird that ny fever broke within 12 hours.

real_comments.comment: Can you contact whoever performed the surgical abortion? Or your OBGYN? It could be a coincidence, but especially with the negative flu test I think it’s best to be cautious. There’s always a risk of infection after surgery and they can be pretty nasty. If your fever spikes again or you’re not feeling good today, I would have a very low threshold to go seek emergency care.

DG.comment: It's good that you have a follow-up appointment scheduled. Any fever after a procedure is worth getting checked out. If the fever returns or you develop worsening pain, heavy bleeding, or foul-smelling discharge, you should contact the clinic sooner rather than waiting for your appointment.

SAG.comment: A fever that high after a procedure is concerning for infection, even if it has since resolved. I'd recommend trying to be seen sooner than your scheduled appointment on Friday.

SAGII.comment: It's good the fever broke, but a fever this high after a procedure is a reason to be seen. Keep the appointment for Friday, but if the fever returns or you develop worsening pain, you should seek care sooner.

title: 30 year old male experiencing some anxiety occasionally at night. If taking Xanax once a week for 2 months can cause dependence
body:
Hello I have a very stressful night at least once a week and I have been taking .75mg at night about once a week, if not less. I was wondering if this can cause dependence and withdrawal symptoms.

This is leftover prescription that I have never needed to refill.

real_comments.comment: No, taking a one dose of alprazolam once weekly will not cause chemical dependence.

DG.comment: At that frequency, it's very unlikely to cause physical dependence or significant withdrawal symptoms. The bigger concern with benzodiazepines is the potential for developing a psychological reliance on them for anxiety.

SAG.comment: Physical dependence and withdrawal are very unlikely with that frequency of use. Those issues typically arise with daily, consistent dosing over a period of time.

SAGII.comment: Physical dependence and withdrawal symptoms are very unlikely with once-weekly use. That's a pattern we typically see with daily use over several weeks to months.

title: Numbness after surgery (2022 Aug)
body:
19f had knee surgery back in August of 22, long story short I’ve had an area of general skin numbness which was checked by my surgeon post op and he said it was nothing of concern. 

Suddenly, I am experiencing tenderness in the area, not the knee but the skin, so much so that I thought I had bruised (wouldn’t be the first, depth perception issues and corners don’t match well). Could my nerves be healing? If so that’s super cool.

real_comments.comment: What surgery? Where is the numbness? Nerves generally "heal" at a rate of 1 mm per day but this is far out enough where it's probably not going to change much

DG.comment: Tenderness in a previously numb area post-surgery is often a sign of nerve regeneration. It's a good sign, even if it's uncomfortable for a bit.

SAG.comment: Yes, it's quite possible this is related to nerve regeneration. As the nerves wake up, they can be hypersensitive for a period of time, which can manifest as tenderness.

SAGII.comment: It's quite possible this is nerve regeneration. As the small nerves that were cut during surgery begin to heal, it's common to experience strange sensations like tenderness, tingling, or zapping feelings in the area that was previously numb.

title: My husband is showing signs of severe mental illness. How can I help him?
body:
39M, located in central Canada, no medications, alcoholic for 10+ years, not sure if thismedical history is relevant but I’ll include it anyway: colitis, IBS, alcoholism, brachial plexus injury, he is 5’8” and extremely thin at around 115lbs. 

I’m not quite sure where to start, but I feel helpless.  My husband has an alcoholic for at least the last 10 years. He was sober for one year in the last 10, then relapsed and has been on and off since.

In mid December, he went on a four day bender and ended it by checking himself into a centre for addiction and mental health after threatening suicide, they kept him for 24 hours, keeping him medicated on Valium and infused what I believe was Thiamine and b12 (I could be wrong). After 24 hours, they no longer deemed him to be a danger to himself or others, and released him with a prescription for naltrexone.  

Just to backpedal a little bit (sorry I am not good at writing so I hope I’m making some sense here), for the past 10 years, he has been held at a hospital on mental health forms, at least five times a year. He threatens suicide constantly. I have called 911 multiple times. He has called 911 on himself multiple times. He calls help lines, they call 911. It just goes on and on. He is always under the influence of alcohol when this happens. Every single time, they tell him if he stops drinking, things will get better. They never address any sort of mental illness or problem.

After his stay and release in December with the naltrexone prescription, he seemed to be doing Ok. Sleeping a lot, not eating much, pretty irritable, but sober and better than I’ve seen him in years. He stayed on naltrexone for about a month, before abruptly, stopping the pills, telling me that they made him feel like he wanted to hurt people and himself, and sure enough, has begun drinking again. 

For the past week, it seems like he is almost in a manic/psychosis, even upon waking. He is convinced he’s being followed by the government, he refuses to bathe, he refuses to eat. He goes on rants about things that don’t make sense, almost as if he’s talking to someone that isn’t there. I caught him talking to a painting we have hung in our living room. 

I have witnessed this behaviour from him before, particularly over the last five years and have always thought he gets into some kind of alcohol induced psychosis, I’m not sure if that is even a thing. When he’s sober, including when he was sober for a year, I would describe him as a depressed person. He did go to the doctor in the year he was sober to get on some sort of antidepressant, but he took it for a week and then refused to take them anymore.

I just don’t know how to get him the help he needs without packing my son up and leaving. I have talked on the phone to doctors during his hospital stays and begged them to keep him and do a full psychiatric work up on him, but they always inform me that once he sobers up, he seems fine and that they can’t legally keep him.

I’m just at a loss on what to do and what is happening to him. Is this Korsakoff syndrome? Is alcohol induced psychosis a thing? Schizophrenia? Will this all disappear if he stays sober? How do you reason with someone that behaves like this and convince them to get help and follow through with the help? I know you can’t force alcoholics to get sober, they have to want to do it for themselves. Is this just pure laziness on his part? Reaching out for help and then not following through? A doctor once told me, and I can’t forget the word he used to describe it, that he is the type of person that enjoys having all the attention on him. I’m not sure if the doctor was alluding to the possibility that he was doing some of this for attention, which I might agree with sometimes, considering he would send pictures of his hospital rooms or his restraints to me and all of his friends. Is this not mental illness at all and just alcoholism?

For what it’s worth, his mother was diagnosed with Schizophrenia shortly after she gave birth to him at 28 years old. 

Thank you anyone for your time and I am sorry that none of this is probably in order. I am just frustrated, concerned and scared wife.

real_comments.comment:
Shitty situation. He's lucky to have had you by his side through all this. Sorry it's been so hard. 


It could well be he has something like bipolar depression, and has been self treating for years incorrectly with alcohol. At that point, from a diagnostic prespective, it's hard to tease apart without him being sober for a time. The technically true but also short way out is to shrug and say "sobriety first" but perhaps a psychiatrist specializing in addiction would have more a more nuanced approach. Hard to rule out something alcohol induced but that's sure not helping things. Korsakoff tends to occur in the absence of eating, and he's quite thin, so it's possible. 


An er visit and admission may be needed to tease this all out.

Hey OP, jesus this is a hard situation.  
The differential is BROAD here:  
\-Yes, it could be Korsokoffs, this is not unheard of in the late 30s. Often age of diagnosis is 45, so he's not far off. -Yes, it could be alcohol-induced psychosis.   
\-He could have delirium, which occurs with confusion and can have hallucinations. This is generally related to a medical problem, which could be anything.  
\-Hepatic encephalopathy is brain inflammation caused by liver failure, and could be at play here.  
\-I could not rule out schizophrenia, but that would be the lowest thing on my list. Schizophrenia tends to present with 6+ months of a change in personality/energy levels/poorer overall functioning/social withdrawal, THEN hallucinations. It is literally impossible to say whether he has this, since he is constantly drinking which makes it hard to identify whether the deterioration is from mental health or from alcohol.

If they discharge him from hospital every time he sobers up, my best guess is that it is alcohol-induced psychosis, which resolves quickly once he stops drinking. That does not change the fact that he could develop Korsokoffs, delirium, hepatic encephalopathy, schizophrenia or any number of other mental health conditions at this point in time. The doctor who told you he is likely doing some of this for attention, is probably suggesting your husband has borderline personality disorder, narcissistic personality disorder, or antisocial personality disorder. Untreated and with active substance use such as in this case, none of these conditions improve substantially and they can be extremely destructive to the people around them.

Unfortunately there is no way of knowing whether this will disappear when he sobers up, since he declines to or is unable to do so. It is not possible for anyone to predict whether he is declining to do so, or is unable to do so. You are correct that you cannot force someone to seek treatment they do not want.

The real question is: what do you want? What do you want for yourself, and your son? No doubt your husband is suffering, but he also: refuses to complete treatment, refuses to take medications, refuses to stop drinking, and is revelling in posting photos of himself in hospital rooms. This is NOT normal or healthy behaviour, and it sets a dangerous example for your child (who is probably terrified watching your husband drink into oblivion, talk to paintings, and have 911 visit the house). This situation is really about you and your son, not your husband, who will likely continue to make his own terrible, repetitive decisions over and over, since that is what he has demonstrated time and time again. When people show you who they are, believe them. You will need to decide who you are, and how you want your child to be raised. 

This is not an easy path. There are a million things on your mind and a million factors impacting your decisions. You have been through the ringer and deserve accolades for holding it together this long. But you're at a crossroads, and I highly recommend caution in your decisions about what company to keep, and who to allow into your life while you try to raise a child to become a healthy and well-adjusted adult.

Godspeed, OP! I hope you can find the peace you deserve.

DG.comment: Yes, alcohol-induced psychosis is a recognized condition. It can involve paranoia and hallucinations and can occur both during heavy drinking and during withdrawal.
The family history of schizophrenia is a very significant piece of information. That, combined with his symptoms, warrants a thorough psychiatric evaluation.

His extremely low weight and refusal to eat in the context of chronic alcoholism is a major red flag for Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. The thiamine he received was to prevent this, but the risk is ongoing.
It's extremely difficult to untangle a primary psychotic disorder from a substance-induced one while the person is still actively using. They often exist together and exacerbate one another.
His current symptoms, especially talking to inanimate objects and paranoid delusions, are severe. The fact that they're present even upon waking is particularly concerning.

The revolving door you're describing is a frustrating reality. The legal criteria for holding someone involuntarily are very strict, and once the acute crisis or intoxication resolves, hospitals often have no legal grounds to keep them.
While some of his actions might seem performative, it doesn't rule out a severe underlying illness. Behavior that seems attention-seeking can be a symptom in itself.
This is a very difficult and volatile situation. It's important to have a safety plan in place for you and your son.

A key diagnostic question is what symptoms persist after a prolonged period of sobriety. If the psychosis remains weeks after he stops drinking, it's more likely a primary psychotic disorder like schizophrenia.
The report that naltrexone made him feel like hurting people is an unusual side effect, but mood changes or dysphoria can occur. It's also possible this was a justification to return to drinking.
It might be helpful to document specific behaviors, delusions, and disorganized speech with dates and times. This can provide a clearer picture for healthcare providers than a general description.

SAG.comment: It's nearly impossible to distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from an alcohol-induced one while someone is actively drinking. The family history of schizophrenia is significant, but a prolonged period of sobriety is necessary to get a clear clinical picture.

It can be very difficult to distinguish between a primary psychotic disorder and an alcohol-induced psychosis when someone is actively drinking. The family history of schizophrenia is a very significant risk factor that needs to be considered.

The family history of schizophrenia is very significant. It can be incredibly difficult to distinguish between a primary psychotic disorder and a substance-induced psychosis without a prolonged period of sobriety.

Alcohol-induced psychosis is very much a real thing, but given his family history and the severity of his symptoms, it's difficult to distinguish from a primary psychotic disorder like schizophrenia without a prolonged period of sobriety.

The family history of schizophrenia is very significant here, especially with the onset of these psychotic symptoms. It can be very difficult to tease apart a primary psychotic disorder from a substance-induced psychosis, particularly with such a long history of heavy alcohol use.

The family history of schizophrenia is very significant here. Substance use can often be a complicating factor or even a trigger for an underlying psychotic illness in genetically predisposed individuals.

It's incredibly difficult to differentiate a primary psychotic disorder from alcohol-induced psychosis while someone is actively using. The symptoms often overlap completely, which is why a prolonged period of sobriety is usually required to make an accurate diagnosis.

The family history of schizophrenia is very significant here. It is often impossible to distinguish a primary psychotic disorder from a substance-induced one without a prolonged period of documented sobriety.

It's extremely difficult to tease apart a primary psychiatric illness from substance-induced psychosis when someone is actively using. The symptoms can look identical, which is why sobriety is often the first necessary step for an accurate diagnosis and effective treatment plan.

It's incredibly difficult to tease apart a primary psychotic disorder from a substance-induced one without a significant period of sobriety. The symptoms can be identical, and the alcohol use will almost always exacerbate any underlying condition.

Alcohol-induced psychosis is very much a real thing. Given his family history, however, it can be extremely difficult to tell if this is purely from the alcohol or an underlying psychotic disorder like schizophrenia being unmasked by the substance use.

SAGII.comment: It's extremely difficult to differentiate a primary psychotic disorder from alcohol-induced psychosis when someone is actively drinking. The strong family history of schizophrenia is very significant here, as substance use disorders are unfortunately very common in people with this condition.

His refusal to eat or bathe due to his current mental state could be considered 'grave disability.' This is often a criterion for an involuntary psychiatric hold, which might allow for a more thorough workup than his previous visits.

Given his history of alcoholism and very low body weight, Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome should be a strong consideration. It's a brain disorder caused by a severe deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1) that can present with psychosis and confusion. This is a medical emergency that requires aggressive vitamin replacement.

This sounds incredibly stressful and frightening for you and your son. Please make sure you're seeking support for yourself through this. Al-Anon is a resource specifically for families and friends of alcoholics that you may find helpful.

His description of naltrexone making him feel like he wanted to hurt himself or others sounds like severe dysphoria, which is a known side effect for some people. There are other medications to help reduce alcohol cravings, such as acamprosate, that work differently and may be an option if he decides to seek treatment again.

To your question about whether this will disappear with sobriety: it's complicated. If it's purely alcohol-induced psychosis, the symptoms should resolve with sustained abstinence. However, with the strong family history, it's very possible there's an underlying primary thought disorder which would require its own separate treatment, independent of the alcoholism.

The strong family history is a very loud signal here. It is not at all uncommon for a primary psychotic illness to be masked for years by a severe substance use disorder, which often significantly delays a formal diagnosis.

With his long history of alcoholism and severe malnutrition, hepatic encephalopathy should also be on the list of possibilities. This is a condition where severe liver dysfunction causes a buildup of toxins in the blood that can lead to profound confusion, personality changes, and psychosis.

This is a classic 'dual diagnosis' problem, and it's a huge gap in our healthcare systems. The ER stabilizes the acute issue and sends him to addiction resources, but the addiction resources aren't equipped for the severe psychosis, and mental health services may not take him while he's actively using. It's an incredibly frustrating cycle for families.

The behavior you're describing, such as seeking help but not following through, isn't necessarily a conscious choice or 'laziness.' It's often a direct symptom of severe mental illness and addiction, reflecting a profound lack of insight into the severity of his own condition.

When you next have to seek emergency care for him, try to have a concise written summary of these specific new psychotic symptoms—the paranoia, talking to paintings, refusal to eat—along with his very low weight and the strong family history of schizophrenia. Presenting this clear, factual information to the ER staff can sometimes help them see beyond the immediate intoxication and advocate for a more comprehensive evaluation.

title: Help with weed
body: I 18m dk where else to go, i only smoked for a year and now i have really bad psychosis and last time i smoked i greened out because it was laced!! i was just curious on how long the effects last, it was really bad and i still feel dissociated, this happened a month a go

real_comments.comment:
If you are susceptible to psychosis from Cannabis you can become psychotic from Cannabis -- doesn't have to be laced.  

The effects can last far longer than the amount of time the Cannabis stays in your system.

Think of it like a light switch.  Your finger turns on the switch, and then you no longer have your finger on the switch, but the light stays on (until it burns out). 

I typically have patients who become psychotic after Cannabis, or any substance, take an antipsychotic for 6 months, then begin reducing the dosage over the next several months. 

One of several things can happen: 

1.  Psychosis "stays gone" and the patient lives life as normal. 

2.  Psychosis leaves, patient tries Cannabis or other substance again, psychosis returns. 

3.  Psychosis remains despite 6 months treatment and sobriety.  Treat for another 6 months and try again.  At 12 months consider the condition chronic and needing long-term treatment. 

I would recommend you stay away from all substances, see a psychiatrist, and figure out what needs to be done for life-long sobriety.  

Some people can play around with substances and end up alright in the long run--you don't seem to be in that group of people.

DG.comment: For symptoms like psychosis and dissociation to persist for a month after you stopped using is significant. These are not typical prolonged effects of cannabis.

Cannabis use, especially at your age, can sometimes trigger or unmask an underlying vulnerability to psychosis. What you're experiencing may be more than just the lingering effects of a laced product.

SAG.comment: New-onset psychosis in a young person, especially in the context of cannabis use, needs to be taken very seriously. It's crucial to abstain from all substances while you get this sorted out.
Persistent psychosis and dissociation for a month after cannabis use is concerning, especially at your age. These types of symptoms often require treatment to resolve.

SAGII.comment: For symptoms like psychosis and dissociation to persist for a month after last use is concerning. This is beyond the acute effects of cannabis and something you should get checked out to understand what's happening.

In some people, particularly in this age group, cannabis can unmask or precipitate a primary psychotic disorder. When that happens, the symptoms don't necessarily resolve just because the drug has worn off.

title: How do the relationships between psychologists, psychiatrists and primary care doctors work?
body:
I understand the main differences of the three and know that a psychologist helps with talk/behavioral therapy while medical doctors and psychiatrists help with medication management and are the ones who can prescribe medication. But how does it work if you feel you need all 3? Do they work with each other? Do psychologists make medication referrals? Do they normally work directly with a psychiatrist? Do you need both or can the psychologist make the referral to your PCP and they can prescribe it without involving a psychiatrist? How does figuring out the best course of action work?

For example, I (F35) am already on stimulants for ADHD, which was diagnosed. I am not officially diagnosed with anxiety and depression, however I expressed my issues to my doctor and he then prescribed me antidepressants (we’ve tried a few) as well as a small amount of anti-anxiety medication at times. My PCP has been my doctor for 15 years.

Recently I’ve been struggling harder than ever and realized I had some deeper issues to sort out. I have my first therapy appointment next week with a psychologist. I feel strongly that I will benefit from talk/behavioral therapy they offer. However I realize they cannot prescribe medication.

I’m fairly certain I need to be medicated but not sure of the correct med combo for what I’m struggling with. I know a psychiatrists specializes in this and can prescribe medication but doesn’t necessarily have the same approach to treatment as psychologists do.

Trying to have a better understanding of the differences/relationships and how this all works. Thank you!

real_comments.comment:
This explanation will get complicated really quick, and there will be a lot of comments likely after my post disagreeing with some part of it.  (For good reason, it isn't something easy to explain.)

Psychologists often don't provide therapy.  A good number of them administer tests and interpret the results.  In some states, a psychologist can prescribe medication.  A mistake in my opinion, but it is what it is.  Patients often say they are seeing a psychologist when in reality they are seeing a therapist. 

Social Workers, Counselors, in some states anyone with a closely related degree (even schoolteachers) can take various tests, do an internship, and then become certified counselors.  These people end up providing therapy.  Not saying this is wonderful, ideal, etcetera, it is just what happens.  Some of these therapists are highly trained and extremely helpful, some aren't.   

Family Doctors, OB-GYNs, some Internal Medicine doctors, occasionally neurologists, provide a huge bulk of psychiatric care.  Some of the doctors in some of these specialties primarily do Mental Health (psychiatric) treatment and nothing else. 

Psychiatrists do psychiatry--treat mental disorders.  Last time I checked as a specialty we are the shortest specialty, meaning we need a huge number of more of us to be able to fill the need.  I was 100% booked the day I started work after training and have never had an issue getting enough patients. True for me and most psychiatrists. 

Doctors are busy--all of them.  If I talk to a primary care provider, a psychologist, or a therapist, usually it is by reading their notes, or one of my nurses talking to their nurse, or by a referral letter, or by a letter from me to the primary care provider.  If it's a direct conversation it is usually short and only occurs once for a given patient.   

The idea that doctors are sitting in a room discussing a case only occurs in residency (training) and at the Department of Veterans Affairs hospitals (because no matter what someone working there tells you, they really aren't that busy).  Everyone else is just trying to keep running on that treadmill until their legs give out for the day. 

 In addition to psychiatrists (MD or DO), there are ARNPs -- Psychiatric Nurse Practitioners.  Some of these can be pretty good--a good number of them aren't, and treatment becomes a circus of different medications and confusion.  (This isn't unique to mental health; there is a great number of this occurring throughout various specialties.)

All 3 of these individuals can have a range of skills sets based on experience and comfort level, which may make it challenging to exactly pinpoint who you should use for each role.

Psychologist - This PhD level training allows them to provide talk therapy, however some also provide neuropsychological testing. They are qualified to diagnose mental health conditions and can piece apart differences of similar diagnoses. Some people schedule weekly therapy, while others see this individual only a few times for evaluation.

Primary Care Physician- Your main point of contact for medical issues. Each PCP may have different levels of comfort with prescribing psychiatric medication. Some will only prescribe SSRIs, others will prescribe for conditions able to be managed by a single medication. When you need multiple medications, or have a complex condition, that is usually when PCP will refer out to psychiatry. 

Psychiatrist- Manages complex psychiatric conditions and medication interactions. When someone has multiple psychiatric diagnosed, such as ADHD, anxiety, and depression, the psychiatrist will have a greater understanding of how medications interact with each other to affect you. 

Given you are already on a stimulant and want to add a second medication for a second condition, seeing a psychiatrist is a reasonable next step.

DG.comment: Ideally, all three providers work as a team. You'll likely be asked to sign a release of information so your psychologist can communicate with your PCP and/or a psychiatrist. This allows them to coordinate your care and make sure everyone is on the same page.

Your new psychologist can certainly make a recommendation for a medication evaluation or adjustment. They would typically send their notes and reasoning to your PCP, who can then make the final prescribing decision or refer you to a psychiatrist if needed.

It's very common for a PCP to manage medications for ADHD, anxiety, and depression. A referral to a psychiatrist is often made if the case is complex, multiple medications haven't worked, or if the PCP feels a specialist's input would be beneficial.

SAG.comment: It's very common for all three to work as a team. With your permission, your new psychologist can communicate their diagnostic impressions and progress to your PCP, which helps them make more informed decisions about medication management.

Yes, we ideally work as a team. Your new psychologist can send their assessment and recommendations to your PCP. If your medication needs become more complex, your PCP might then refer you to a psychiatrist for specialized management while you continue therapy.

Yes, we often work collaboratively. Your new psychologist can communicate with your PCP about medication recommendations, or they might suggest a referral to a psychiatrist if your case is more complex.

SAGII.comment: Your psychologist can absolutely send a letter to your PCP with their diagnostic impressions and recommendations for medication. Many PCPs are comfortable managing these meds, but may also refer you to a psychiatrist if your case is more complex.

It's a great team-based approach. Your psychologist's input after a few sessions can be incredibly valuable to your PCP or a psychiatrist when it comes to fine-tuning medications. You'll just need to sign a release of information form for them to be able to communicate directly about your care.

Your psychologist can definitely coordinate with your PCP. That said, given you're dealing with ADHD in addition to anxiety and depression, your PCP may ultimately feel more comfortable having a psychiatrist manage your medications. It allows for a more specialized approach to finding the right combination of meds to support the work you're doing in therapy.

real_comments.comment: Hi there - I highly suggest contacting poison control and your doctor. The biggest issue with taking high amounts of vitamin D is that vitamin D also raises your calcium level. DG.comment: That's a very high dose, but it would be unusual to see toxicity after only 12 days. The most important thing is to stop taking it now and contact your doctor's office when they open to let them know.
Nausea can be a symptom of high vitamin D levels, but it's very non-specific and could easily be from your anxiety about the situation. Make sure you stay well-hydrated.
When you speak to your doctor, they will likely order some bloodwork to check your vitamin D and calcium levels to make sure everything is okay.

Yes, that is a very high dose. Stop taking it immediately. You should contact your doctor to have your vitamin D and calcium levels checked. In the meantime, make sure you are staying well hydrated.

title: Recurrent thrush and contraception

real_comments.comment:
Hi there, Doctor here,

Firstly, have you noticed a correlation or cause for the thrush? For example, can you be confident that the thrush appeared after you started oral contraception? When did you very first start oral contraceptives and when did you get your first thrush infection? Have you noticed any correlation between thrush and sexual partners? 

It would be useful if you could answer the above questions.

Generally speaking, there is a potential increased risk of thrush when taking oral contraceptives (both combined and “mini” pill). To my understanding, this is generally uncommon. 
If you are confident that this is the cause however, a good option to consider would be a non hormonal IUD or a progestin IUD (eg. Mirena IUD). These generally have a more localised hormonal affect and don’t impact the vaginal tissues as much. 

I hope this helps at least a little.

I’m happy to answer any questions.

Kind regards.

DG.comment: Some people find that progestin-only methods (like the mini-pill, implant, or a hormonal IUD) are less problematic than combined methods. A non-hormonal copper IUD is also an excellent long-term option if you want to avoid hormones altogether.

SAG.comment: Your doctor's plan to trial a break from hormonal contraception is a good one to see if there's a link. If you do find hormones are a trigger, non-hormonal options like the copper IUD are very effective. Some people also do better on progesterone-only methods, which don't contain estrogen.

SAGII.comment: The copper IUD is an excellent non-hormonal option. Some people also do well with progestin-only methods like a hormonal IUD or the implant, as the link with thrush is less established than with estrogen.

title: Major Female Urinary Retention
body: 46 yo female. A little health background. Full colostomy at 31 for UC which left a ton of scar tissue, hysterectomy at 42 for cervix literally coming out of me, and recently an 11cm cyst found after an MRI done for my retention (but docs don’t think it’s affecting my pee). Also avid beer drinker for years now, but not a crazy amount at a time. Ok, February 14th 2025. My husband and I were at our local brewery and I had the need to pee badly. Only a trickle. Had that feeling all night and just a trickle until we finally had to go to the ER. Over 1 liter was catheterized out of me at the time. Had to keep that in until the Monday when I could see a urologist. They kept saying if I were a man they’d know the issue… took the catheter out and said let’s see what happens. That very next Friday, in the ER again. 2 liters this time. Multiple Cather bags because I still just couldn’t pee. MRIs, flow studies, changed to a female urologist (which was amazing to not hear “if you were a man”), learned to self catheterize. Quit drinking for a while, which did somewhat help, but my bladder never fully empties no matter what. Finally decided to do the Axonics surgery after meds and PT for pelvic floor. The trial wasn’t great, but was told that it takes longer than 2 weeks for retention. Well, I’m almost 4 months in and I see a little improvement with the feeling of having to pee, but still have to catheterize every 2 weeks-ish. At this point, I’m considering having this removed as it’s a foreign object in my body and it hasn’t made a huge difference. Any help or suggestions or anything appreciated. I think my bladder never fully empties and it just builds. I don’t mind self catheterizing, but worried about UTIs and whatever else comes with that. Help! I’m lost and my urologist seems to be too.

real_comments.comment:
What medications are you taking (all of them for all conditions)?  

If not a medication issue, I'd suggest a neurologist evaluation -- a neurologic issue can either cause incontinence or retention.

DG.comment: With your history of extensive pelvic surgeries, including the colectomy and hysterectomy, it's highly possible that there has been some nerve damage affecting bladder function. This can be a very challenging and complex issue to manage.

SAG.comment: Has your urologist considered video urodynamics? It can provide a much clearer picture of what's happening with your bladder muscle versus the outlet, especially given your complex surgical history.

SAGII.comment: Your extensive surgical history likely plays a major role. It might be worth seeking a second opinion from a specialist in female pelvic medicine and reconstructive surgery (a urogynecologist) or a neuro-urologist, as these can be very complex cases.

SAG.comment: A daily antimicrobial wash like benzoyl peroxide 10% or chlorhexidine can be very helpful for reducing recurrence in those areas. It helps decrease the bacterial colonization that contributes to the flares.

SAGII.comment: An antimicrobial wash like chlorhexidine or benzoyl peroxide can be very helpful for long-term management to reduce bacterial load. You're also right to focus on weight loss, as that is a key component for many people.

title: Breaking medications to smaller sizes
body:
Hello everyone , couldn't find a place to ask a pharmacist so here it goes. 

Male, late 70s, stage 4 lung cancer and swallowing issues. I'm wondering if it is okay to break up his medications into smaller sizes and give those with apple sauce and such. However cannot find definitive answers. The medications I'm wondering about are Bactrim , Atorvastatin and Prednisone.  Thanks for any help.

real_comments.comment:
Whether medications can be crushed depends on at least two issues: 

1.  Is the medication acid-sensitive?  If it is, then stomach acid can destroy the medication. 

2.  Is it delayed/controlled release?  If it is, then crushing the medicine turns it into immediate release which may drastically change its short-term dosage and effects. 

* Bactrim can be safely crushed -- not acid sensitive and not delayed release.
* Atorvastatin can't be crushed -- acid sensitive and stomach acid can destroy this medication. I would ask the physician prescribing this if this medication needs continued, given the person has Stage IV lung cancer. 
* Prednisone -- depends on whether it is immediate or controlled-release.  Should be on the label, if the label doesn't say, it is likely immediate-release and can be crushed.  Any doubts, call the pharmacy and ask if immediate or controlled/delayed release.

DG.comment: Prednisone and immediate-release atorvastatin can generally be crushed. Bactrim can be as well, but it has a famously unpleasant taste that's hard to mask. It may be easier to ask the pharmacy if any of his medications are available in a liquid formulation.

SAG.comment: Prednisone and atorvastatin are fine to crush. The Bactrim is too, but it has a very strong bitter taste. It also comes in a liquid suspension which might be a better option.

SAGII.comment: Prednisone and Bactrim both come in liquid formulations which would be much easier. It's worth asking the prescribing doctor or pharmacy if they can switch him to those.

title: Caffeine Shivers

SAG.comment: The description, especially that it becomes more prominent when you put pressure on the foot, is very suggestive of a plantar fibroma. It's not an urgent concern, so your appointment next week is fine.

SAGII.comment: Could be a number of things, but common possibilities include a ganglion cyst or a plantar fibroma. Unless it's acutely painful, growing rapidly, or the overlying skin is changing, waiting for your appointment next week is reasonable.

title: Upper Hip Pain (32F)
body:
Like the title says, I’m 32F and I’ve been having pain in my upper left hip (like love handle area) for the last month or so. I thought it might be a muscle strain so I initially iced it as well as applied heat and soaked in the tub. I thought it was getting better but this last week it’s gotten worse. It’s more of a sharp pain than a dull pain and sometimes I can feel it more when I take steps.

Only vitamin I take is folic acid because it was low the last time I got my bloods done. Don’t smoke and only have maybe a glass of wine or two a month. 

Just wondering if this is something more than a strain and if I should head to urgent care tomorrow! If not, I’ll make a regular appt on Monday but sometimes it can take over a week to get an appt and I don’t want it to keep getting worse. Thank you in advance!

real_comments.comment: It sounds appropriate for a GP/PCP and not urgent care workup. If you have fevers or an inability to walk on it, then urgent care.

DG.comment: Pain in that specific area often originates from the gluteal muscles, like the gluteus medius, but can also be referred from the lower back or sacroiliac joint. Since it's been a month and is worsening, getting a physical exam with your regular doctor is a reasonable next step.

SAG.comment: Pain in the 'love handle' area can often be referred from your lower back or SI joint. Given that it's getting worse and making it hard to walk, getting it evaluated soon is a good idea.

SAGII.comment: Pain in that specific location, especially when sharp and worse with walking, can sometimes be referred from your lower back or sacroiliac joint rather than the hip joint itself. See if you can reproduce the pain by pressing on the bony parts of your lower back or upper buttock.

title: Got stitches on Tuesday 10/21 and am leaving for a vacation on 10/31 where I won't have access to good medical care. Looking for advice on managing the wound and sutures.
body:
41M, good overall health. I was in a bike accident on Tuesday where I hit a pothole at a pretty good speed and went over the handle bars and have scapes and cuts all of my body. The worst of it was my left knee which was torn open badly enough that there was fat and/or tendon exposed. I received 8 soutures in that knee and 2 in my left elbow as well as minor road rash on several other parts of my body.

I'm getting on a flight on 10/31 and then onto a cruise ship on 11/1. Since the soutures are supposed to come out sometime between 10/31 and 11/4 (10-14 days), and I'll be on the ship at this time, I'm looking for advice on a plan of action. The doctor at the ER really didn't give me much advice because they said that the plan of action would be TBD depending on how healing is going. Advice they gave me was to bandage with gauze pads and bacitracin until the wound is staying dry.

I also plan to go to urgent care on 10/30 in the evening for evaluation.

Assuming the doctor at urgent care doesn't take out the soutures 9.5 days after the accident, what is my best plan for having them removed? Should I have the ship's doctor do it? Do it myself using a sterile medical scissors (I've done this before a couple of times with no issues)? Leave them in until I can have them removed on 11/10?

What should I avoid doing water wise both before and after the soutures come out? I have some tegaplast that I was going to use for water activities to try to be safe and was planning on putting some butterfly bandages over the knee after the stitches come out to try to minimize the risk of it reopening. Any types of water I should avoid specifically (e.g. hot tubs, the ocean)? Should I ask an MD to write an RX for an antibiotic in case it gets infected on the cruise? I'm also pretty sure I have some cephalexin sitting around somewhere that I was planning on bringing, but it's probably 2 years old or so.

real_comments.comment:
To be clear, the safest answer if to not go on the trip. I know it's not what you want to hear but it is.

That being said, just leave the incision uncovered and clean with soap and water I'm the shower daily. 

Do not submerge your incisions while on the cruise at all.

I wouldn't appy bacitracin or anything to it. Maybe seeing it would change my mind, maybe not.

Just leave the sutures in until you return. I wouldn't get them removed at UC before you leave.

And just monitor for infection on the cruise. If you think it's getting infected, visit the ship's doctor.

All the best!

DG.comment: Leaving sutures in over a joint for that long is not ideal, as it increases the risk of scarring and makes them harder to remove. I would plan on having the ship's doctor take them out. Definitely do not take old, expired antibiotics; they are likely ineffective and not indicated here anyway.

SAG.comment: Leaving the sutures in until you return is often preferable for a wound over a joint. Taking them out too early, especially on the knee, risks the wound dehiscing (opening up). Definitely do not try to remove them yourself.

SAGII.comment: Sutures over a joint like the knee should ideally stay in for a full 14 days to minimize the risk of the wound opening. Leaving them in until you return on 11/10 is likely the safest course of action.

sheet_name: 45. How to deal with a doctor'
title: How to deal with a doctor's apparent inherent bias and a potential missed diagnosis?
body:
Almost 40F. No tobacco or drug use but I do drink. Only very occasionally to the point of drunk, but daily. Usually one if I eat lunch out and a couple in the evening. I realize it's not the best, but I always take a month off each year and I can cut down and I've never experienced withdrawal symptoms, aside from slightly increased anxiety. I've made large strides in the last several years on my anxiety and I don't think I'm using it pathologically. I don't have kids and I'm retired, so I'm just living a lifestyle that didn't have much in the way of consequences.



I just saw my PCP for extreme weight loss (175-150, 5'6", stable weight for 20 years), nausea, vomiting, fatigue, bruising, blah blah blah. Except I never got the chance to get to my symptoms. She just heard alcohol use and totally jumped down my throat. My medical notes made me cry. 



She at least ordered labs and a GI referral. I got my labs back and there's a few things that were abnormal, including my AST and T-Bili are just out of normal range. 

  
Because it's Thanksgiving, I got a follow-up from someone else. It mentioned it's probably alcohol but he's going to order some additional testing. Those came back and my ferritin is >1000 and the saturation thing is 95%. I'm waiting on genetic labs, but he thinks it's very likely to be hemochromatosis. I'm young, but I've had an IUD and light periods for most of my life. 

  
If in fact I have this, how do I go about addressing this with the office? I feel like her inherent bias could have drastically shortened my lifespan. I'm obviously going to stop drinking and fully comply with all recommendations, but from my understanding, if I don't get treatment while it's still treatable I would be at horrible risk of organ failure and death. I don't want this to happen to someone else. How do I respectfully approach this with the office?

real_comments.comment:
You drink well in excess of what’s considered low risk for a woman, and alcohol-related problems could explain your symptoms. It makes sense for your doctor to address the high-likelihood and modifiable risk factor for your symptoms. 

It’s unclear what “jumped down [your] throat” means but it does seem in this post that you have some denial about your drinking problem and perhaps you’re feeling defensive about her addressing that

I agree with the other comment entirely. 

Quite frankly, the quantity of alcohol consumed is a problem. The average person is not having a drink out at lunch and multiple drinks per night. That is well in excess of what is recommended and very readily could lead to some of the abnormal labs listed above and that amount of alcohol use in the long run will have serious deleterious health impacts. 

I'm also not sure what "bias" you say you experienced. You were referred to a specialist for additional consultation. If they simply thought it was alcohol, you wouldn't necessarily need to see a GI doc. Additional lab testing as a result of the initial lab testing or even through the specialist (which is why people refer to specialists) is to be expected.

DG.comment: Your iron studies are indeed classic for hemochromatosis. It's fortunate the covering clinician thought to check them. The good news is that you are now on the correct diagnostic path and the treatment is very effective.

It's understandable to feel frustrated. One approach is to request a follow-up appointment to specifically discuss the new findings and your care plan. If you've lost trust, it is always your right to establish care with a different primary care provider, even within the same office.

SAG.comment: While your initial labs and symptoms certainly point towards the liver, those iron studies are a huge red flag for hemochromatosis. It's good that the second physician broadened the differential. I would ask to establish care with that physician moving forward.

While alcohol can certainly affect liver enzymes, a ferritin over 1000 with that level of saturation is a huge red flag for hemochromatosis. It's good the follow-up physician ordered the right tests to get you on the correct diagnostic path.

SAGII.comment: Most clinics have a practice manager or patient advocate. You can request a meeting or send a letter to discuss your experience and concerns about the initial consultation. This is often the most effective way to provide feedback.

The alcohol use combined with elevated liver enzymes would make any physician consider alcohol-related liver injury, but it shouldn't be the end of the workup. The very high ferritin and iron saturation are classic for hemochromatosis and definitely warrant the genetic testing. It's good this was caught.

title: Placental pathology after stillbirth
body:
Hi everyone,

We lost our daughter at 27 weeks gestation and I could use some help deciphering the pathology report. I could wait until we have an appointment with a maternal fetal medicine provider but I'm too impatient for that. 



I'm 35F with a history of (very well controlled) Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Very uneventful pregnancy, all testing normal. Took 100 mg Prometrium orally from after ovulation until 13 weeks, then took baby aspirin along with levothyroxine (started at 88 mcg, then increased to 125 mcg, then back down to 112 mcg), prenatal vitamins and dha. Two previous pregnancy losses - 6 week miscarriage followed by an ectopic with ruptured fallopian tube & salpingostomy (June and September 2024). Family history of concealed hemorrhage/placental abruption (mom) at approximately 34 weeks during her pregnancy with me (not sure exactly how many weeks she was at the time).



Placenta:  
Immature placenta, 192 g, at 10th percentile  
Focal hemosiderin deposition within decidua  
Retroplacental hemorrhage  
Involutional vascular changes associated with intrauterine demise  
Intervillous thrombus

  
COMMENT:  
The precise cause of death cannot be established based on isolated  
placental review.  There is no evidence of ascending amniotic fluid  
infection, fetal inflammatory response, fetal vascular malperfusion, or  
chronic villitis.

  
GROSS DESCRIPTION:  
A:  Specimen: Received fresh labeled with the patient's name and  
"placenta" per requisition  
Weight  Disc dimensions: 192 g (at the 10th percentile), 16 x 13.5 x  
1.5 cm  
Umbilical cord: 30 cm long by 1-1.5 cm in diameter, focally dusky,  
trivascular, eccentric insertion approximately 6 cm from the closest  
disc edge  
Membranes: Pink-tan, semitranslucent, marginal insertion  
Fetal surface: Blue-tan with small caliber vessels and scant fibrin  
deposition  
Maternal surface: Red-tan, focally disrupted, possibly incomplete with  
well-formed cotyledons and no calcifications  
Placental parenchyma: Pale, soft and spongy  
Other abnormalities: None identified

Worth noting (I think) that our baby was in the 97th percentile and measuring weeks ahead in all categories - could there have been an issue with the placenta measuring so small in comparison? Our 20 week anatomy scan also noted the umbilical cord as having a "central placental cord origin" - does that contradict the report here as having an eccentric insertion? Or, are they two entirely different things?

  
Thank you.

real_comments.comment: Going to ping u/drewdrewmd as this is their speciality!

DG.comment: I'm so very sorry for your loss. The findings of retroplacental hemorrhage and hemosiderin deposition point to bleeding behind the placenta. When you have a small placenta supporting a large baby, it can create a high-demand situation where the placenta struggles to keep up.

SAG.comment: I'm so sorry for your loss. The retroplacental hemorrhage is a significant finding and essentially means there was a placental abruption. The hemosiderin deposition suggests there may have been some older, chronic bleeding there as well.

SAGII.comment: The retroplacental hemorrhage and intervillous thrombus findings point toward a placental abruption, which is consistent with your mother's history. I'm so very sorry for your devastating loss.

body:

real_comments.comment: What kind of medical professionals? Are any of the people you talked to allergy docs?

DG.comment: The diagnostic criteria for MCAS are quite specific, but the symptoms patients present with are often very non-specific and can overlap with dozens of other conditions. It requires a thorough workup to rule out more common things first, which can be a long process.

It helps to come in with a detailed symptom diary, noting foods, activities, and specific reactions. True MCAS often has objective findings, like changes in blood pressure or flushing, that can be documented. A baseline tryptase level is a common starting point for investigation.

SAG.comment: It's a tricky area because the symptoms are often non-specific and overlap with many other conditions. The best way to approach it is by keeping a detailed symptom and food diary and presenting that data. Objective information is always the most helpful starting point.

It can be more productive to focus on your specific symptoms rather than a potential diagnosis. Describe what you're experiencing, when it happens, and what makes it better or worse. That gives us more concrete information to work with.

SAGII.comment: Focus on your symptoms, not the specific diagnosis you suspect. Bringing a detailed symptom log that includes potential triggers, timing, and severity is often the most productive way to start the conversation.

Part of the issue is that it's a diagnosis of exclusion with a complex workup, and the symptoms are very non-specific. We have to rule out a lot of other, more common things first, which can make it seem like we're being dismissive when we're actually just trying to be methodical.

title: How much chances are that we are pregnant? How can we avoid it?
body:

real_comments.comment: She's still within the window for an IUD (copper or hormonal both work as emergency contraception and would provide ongoing pregnancy prevention); we recommend within 5 days. It's entirely possible the emergency pill she took was effective, but you're correct about the ovulation timing. She'll need to decide if she'd like the secondary/additional protection from an IUD.

DG.comment: A copper IUD is indeed the most effective form of emergency contraception and can be placed up to 5 days after unprotected sex. Given the timing, it would be the best option to maximize the chances of preventing a pregnancy.

SAG.comment: The copper IUD is an excellent option for emergency contraception, and it is the most effective one available. It can be inserted up to 5 days after intercourse, so you are still well within the window for that.

SAGII.comment: A copper IUD is the most effective form of emergency contraception available and can be inserted up to five days after unprotected intercourse. It would be a very reasonable next step to take, especially given the timing in her cycle.

SAGII.comment: Keep it clean with soap and water, apply an antibiotic ointment, and keep it covered with a bandage, especially at work. Watch for redness spreading up the toe or any thick, yellow/green drainage.

title: got blackout drunk, black bits in vomit?
body:
yesterday i (26f) had some vodka with my friend after work (i want to say 5 or 6 shots?). we work very early in the morning so we were drinking around 3pm, and i drank on a mostly empty stomach.

i used to handle that amount fine, but i haven't been drinking for a while and overestimated my tolerance. i last remember feeling a little drunk, then next thing i know i'm waking up on the floor of my bedroom in my own puke hours later. i've only blacked out maybe once or twice in my life so this was really scary to me. 

it is now 4am and i've been up all night puking. called out of work because it just won't stop. what is alarming me besides the blacking out, is at some point there were black chunks in my vomit. at some point in the middle of the night i'd had a diet coke, so my first thought was that, but the vomit was clear with black chunks (some like coffee grounds?) so that was strange to me?

i want to go to urgent care but need to wait until they are open later this morning. am i overreacting? if i go, what exactly should i ask them for, or ask them to look at?

real_comments.comment:
Coffee grounds in vomit are either literal coffee grounds, which seems unlikely, or partially digested blood. 

You can tear the lining of the esophagus with vomiting, leading to either vomiting some blood, or "coffee ground emesis." If the blood gets in the stomach, the stomach acid partially digests it into something that looks like coffee grounds. Then when you throw it up later that's how it looks. 

Could also be a gastric ulcer, or you cut your mouth and were swallowing a lot of blood, or something else. 

If it seems like a lot, or if you feel like something is just plain wrong, go to the emergency room. If you feel fine and it doesn't continue and you don't have any chest or stomach pain, it's probably fine.

DG.comment: Black material in your vomit that looks like coffee grounds can be a sign of bleeding in your stomach. I would recommend going to an emergency room instead of waiting for an urgent care to open.
It's very common to overestimate your tolerance after a period of not drinking. It drops much more quickly than people realize.
Diet Coke wouldn't typically cause black chunks like you're describing, especially in otherwise clear vomit. The appearance of coffee grounds is the most concerning part of your story.

SAG.comment: Vomit that looks like coffee grounds can be a sign of bleeding in your upper GI tract. This is something that warrants a visit to the emergency department rather than waiting for an urgent care to open.

The black material that looks like coffee grounds is concerning for an upper GI bleed from the irritation. If you are still vomiting continuously, you may want to go to the emergency department rather than waiting for urgent care to open.

Vomit that looks like coffee grounds can be a sign of bleeding in your stomach. Given that you're vomiting continuously, I would suggest going to an emergency department rather than waiting for urgent care to open.

SAGII.comment: Vomit that looks like coffee grounds is very concerning and warrants immediate evaluation. I would not wait for urgent care to open; this is a reason to go to the emergency department.

The black specks that look like coffee grounds could be digested blood from your stomach, which can be caused by irritation from the alcohol and vomiting. You should mention that specific detail when you seek care.

When you get evaluated, be sure to describe the vomit exactly as you did here, specifically mentioning the 'coffee grounds' appearance. They will likely want to check your blood counts and assess you for dehydration from all the vomiting.

See your parent or teacher or you need to see a doc.

DG.comment: Difficulty breathing is not something to mess with, especially when your rescue inhaler isn't working. You need to be evaluated in an emergency department immediately.

SAG.comment: Difficulty breathing after swallowing river water, especially when your rescue inhaler provides no relief, is concerning. This could be something like a chemical pneumonitis or a developing infection and needs to be evaluated promptly.

SAGII.comment: Difficulty breathing that doesn't improve with your rescue inhaler warrants an immediate in-person evaluation, especially after swallowing river water.

title: Covid, flu, cold, or something else?
body:

Fever of 102 came on quickly yesterday evening and has lasted today with Advil cutting it and making me feel a little better. Body aches and chills with fever.

Could this be a cold, flu, or Covid, or any of the above? Dr’s office is closed until next week.

real_comments.comment: Any of the above. You can always do a home swab to see if it's COVID/Flu if you want. Nothing here sounds particularly worrisome, so I would just continue self care at home.
