SAG.comment: The sudden onset of high fever, body aches, and chills is very characteristic of influenza, though it's impossible to distinguish from COVID on symptoms alone. A common cold is much less likely to cause that degree of fever.

SAGII.comment: The rapid onset of a high fever with significant body aches is very characteristic of influenza. You'd need to get tested to differentiate it from COVID, as the symptoms overlap significantly.

sheet_name: 58. I may have thrown a clot i
title: I may have thrown a clot in my pulmonary valve stent. What’s my outlook/prognosis?
body:
31F PDA at birth, pulmonary valve replacement 2004, valvuloplasty 2006, pulmonary valve replacement 2021 with a stent and complication of a hemathorax, 2 NSTEMI’s, 2 elevated troponin. Factor five Leiden with a hx of DVT and multiple bilateral PE’s

I was woken up this morning with chest pain. Didn’t think much of it. Went about my usual morning routine. Breakfast. Let the dog out. Take meds. Etc. well I went to shower around 10am and was just washing my hair and my body and got extremely short of breath. Like huffing and puffing bad. It took me a good 40 mins to recover from that. I decided to call 911 and just from walking from the house to the ambulance I couldn’t form a complete sentence. My HR was 144 and stayed around 120’s while on the way to the ED. 

I get here. Get an EKG. The typical blood work up for chest pain. I see the resident physician, explain what had went on and then he said I needed a CTA of my chest since this sounded like another PE. Got my scan and around the stent was well visualized but the stent itself was not. I have had PLENTY of CTA’s and this has never been a finding on them before. So the attending came to talk to me and said he was concerned about me not being able to talk in complete sentences without getting winded and then with my heart rate jumping to 125 with an ambulation trial and how difficult the trial was for me. He was concerned of a clot in my pulmonary valve stent. He reached out to the pulmonologist who agreed with him and they are keeping me here until further notice. 

I’m supposed to have an echo and meet with the pulmonologist and the cardiologist and may even have more tests ran. They’ve started me on lovenox every 12 hours as well. I’m just a little nervous and scared of this situation and looking for some more insight if possible. 

I did miss about 2 days of my eliquis due to moving and was on norethindrone for about three months due to chronic pelvic pain. Figured that would be pertinent info but didn’t know where to put it. 

Any and all insight is appreciated. Thank you.

real_comments.comment: That sounds like a great question for the multiple specialists you are going to be seeing in the very near future who have access to your chart.
You’re in the right place, getting the right medicine, and will be seen by the right specialists. There’s not much else anyone else here will be able to tell you without your chart in front of us

DG.comment: Missing a couple days of your Eliquis is certainly a significant event given your history. Combined with the norethindrone, your risk for a clot would have been quite high. It's good you sought care quickly and they've got you back on anticoagulation.
An echocardiogram is the right next step here. It will give a much better view of the stent and any potential clot or obstruction than the CT. Glad to hear they have a solid plan in place for you.

SAG.comment: Missing a couple of days of Eliquis, especially with your history and Factor V Leiden, could certainly be a contributing factor. Starting you on anticoagulation with Lovenox is the right immediate step while they complete the workup.

Given your history and symptoms, the concern for a clot in your stent is very appropriate. Starting Lovenox immediately is the standard of care. The echo will give a much better look at the valve's function.

SAGII.comment: The plan to get an echo and consults while treating you with Lovenox is exactly the right approach. The echo will give a much better look at the valve and stent than the CT could.

Missing Eliquis doses and taking norethindrone, especially with your Factor V Leiden, is a significant setup for a clot. It's good they started Lovenox immediately while they get the more definitive imaging.

title: 3 week old had viral meningitis (enterovirus) now eczema
body:
Our child had viral meningitis at 3 weeks old and was hospitalised for a short period of time. The child had a fever of over 40 centigrade and was given IV antibiotics for just over 72 hours due to the doctor thinking they had sepsis. The child (4 years old) now has eczema and I have been told it is unlikely tied to a food allergy. Instead, the dietician said, it may be due to the child having a heightened stress response to things such as temperatures, textures, weather changes, etc.

I've been unable to talk with a doctor about the possible long-term impacts on the child of viral meningitis or IV antibiotics at such an early age. I've read one study which suggested that viral meningitis generally does not impact on a child long-term but I don't know how to further research (what to search for) to understand how the hospitalisation/antibiotics/high fever/illness could have impacted on the overall ability for our child to handle stressors like the ones I mentioned above. Can any medical professionals point me toward studies or give me their advice/thoughts? I would like to heal the child's eczema but not sure what to do now if it is not coming from a food allergy. Thanks, very grateful.

real_comments.comment:
Eczema is an extremely common condition without a clear trigger other than a genrally excitable immune system. It is not likely related to the early meningitis/antibiotic exposure, particularly because the time between them is so great.


General eczema treatment is keeping the skin as baseline healthy and moisturized as possible, avoiding potential environmental irritants like dyes, scents,  and products with these in them. Eczema is often worse in winter because of how dry the air is, so a good moisturizer regimen with simple products like aquaphor or Vaseline can help you stay ahead of it.

DG.comment: It's true that for most children, enteroviral meningitis doesn't have long-term neurodevelopmental effects. The link to eczema is less clear, but since eczema is an immune-mediated condition, the focus for treatment remains the same regardless of the trigger: aggressive moisturization to support the skin barrier and topical steroids for flares.

SAG.comment: It's highly unlikely the neonatal meningitis or its treatment is the root cause of your child's eczema four years later. Eczema is an inflammatory condition, often genetic, and while stress or illness can trigger flares, they don't typically cause the underlying condition itself.

SAGII.comment: It's true that significant illnesses and antibiotic use in early infancy can play a role in shaping the developing immune system. This is sometimes linked to the development of atopic conditions like eczema later on, though it's very difficult to prove a direct cause-and-effect relationship from a single event.

title: Low diastolic blood pressure in a young female
body:
Hello, I am very concerned and would appreciate some advice.
I'm a 26 year old female with blood pressure around 110/55. Systolic number is always in the normal range, however diastolic is always lower than "normal". I had an echo and ecg done and no doctor seems to be too concerned. However, every time i get my BP measure at the doctors it's higher then at home (on different monitors too).
Since I also have high anxiety and I always feel dizzy, sleepy confused and short of breath, I can't stop thinking that something is wrong. I am waiting for a table tilt test, but I have that in 10 months.. I sometimes experience palpitations and chest pain too, however as far as I know it could all just be anxiety. 
But my concern is that with low diastolic BP, my heart doesn't get enough oxygen. How would I know if that was the case? I feel bad all the time anyway so I'm symptomatic either way. Google tells me that isolated diastolic hypotension can be very dangerous and I'm terrified of having a stroke or some kind of deadly arrythmia from not gettin enough oxygen. 
So could someone tell me if that kind of blood pressure could just be normal since I'm young and don't have stiff arteries? I'm not an athlete tho, not active at all, but normal weight.
Thank you all in advance.

real_comments.comment: That is a normal BP, nothing to be concerned about. Sounds like it would be beneficial for you to address your anxiety while you wait for the test, likely the highest yield area that will help you the most.

DG.comment: A diastolic pressure in the 50s isn't typically concerning in a young person, especially with a normal systolic pressure and reassuring cardiac tests like an echo and ECG. The concern about the heart not getting enough oxygen (coronary perfusion) is more relevant in older individuals with stiffened arteries or known coronary artery disease.

SAG.comment: For a young, healthy person, a diastolic BP in the 50s is often just a normal variant and not dangerous. The concern for poor coronary perfusion generally comes into play at much lower pressures, especially in the setting of underlying heart disease.

SAGII.comment: The concern about poor coronary perfusion with low diastolic pressure is primarily for older patients with stiff arteries or known coronary artery disease. In a young person with a normal echo and ECG, your heart is very likely getting all the oxygen it needs.

title: Why does my wife’s nose (28F) smell so badly?
body:
My wife broke her nose in college and has had ongoing nasal/sinus issues since then. Over the years she's had multiple surgeries, including one fairly recently, but there's still a very strong, pungent odor coming from her nose. It's noticeable to her and to people close to her.

She's seen multiple ENTs. One mentioned something along the lines of "bacterial exhaust" (his words), but another ENT basically dismissed that as not a real thing. So we're a bit stuck and confused.

She's tried medicated sinus rinses (antibiotic/ steroid rinses) and they don't seem to make any difference at all. No real relief, no change in the smell.

At this point we're just trying to understand: 
• What conditions can cause a persistent foul odor from the nose like this? 
• Are there structural issues, chronic infections, or less obvious causes that sometimes get missed? 
• Is there anything specific we should be asking her ENT to evaluate or test for?

real_comments.comment: Has she had a sinus ct?

DG.comment: Has anyone mentioned the possibility of atrophic rhinitis (ozena)? It can be a complication after multiple nasal surgeries and is known to cause a distinct foul smell.

SAG.comment: Has she had a dental evaluation, including a panoramic x-ray? A chronic odontogenic source (i.e., from a tooth root infection) can sometimes be the culprit for persistent sinus issues and odor.

SAGII.comment: Given her history of multiple surgeries, I would ask her ENT to specifically evaluate for atrophic rhinitis (ozena). It's a condition characterized by atrophy of the nasal lining that can lead to chronic crusting and a very foul odor.

title: 4x size liver, 2 weeks progressive jaundice untreated
body:
Hopefully this is the right sub. I will include as much detail as possible that I believe is relevant, I will explain further if needed.

What’s something to tell a couple about the severity of the situation, and if this is something to “take a rest about.”

Assume these next bits are verified and/or easily observable: Male, early 60s.

1. 14 days since yellowing onset. slight tint in eyes and face until day 12. yellowing became highly visible in eyes face and neck becoming darker shades.

2. Acute mental decline, confusion at times, lethargic. Sleep is short and spontaneous, 2 to 3 weeks now.

3. Life long heavy alcoholic and daily smoker, liver size confirmed end of September and titrated from 5-7 shots + 2-4 large beers to 1 shot + 1 beer. Smoking daily continued as normal, 6-12 cigarettes.

4. Abdomen is noticeably larger while he still loses weight. Barely eating or drinking for 2-3 weeks now, besides the shots obviously just a little bit of juice or protein drink. 

Is the a reversible situation or is he in some late stage illness?

real_comments.comment: Generally late stage liver disease. Sounds like alcoholic hepatitis that may recover a bit. However, 50% of patients with alcoholic hepatitis have end stage liver disease (cirrhosis).

DG.comment: The combination of worsening jaundice and acute mental status changes like confusion and lethargy is a marker of severe, acute liver failure. This is a medical emergency, not something to 'take a rest' about.

SAG.comment: The mental status changes in the setting of progressive jaundice are highly concerning for hepatic encephalopathy, a complication of severe liver failure. This is a medical emergency.

SAGII.comment: The combination of progressive jaundice, abdominal swelling, and especially the acute mental decline are signs of severe, decompensated liver disease. This is a medical emergency and not something to wait on.

sheet_name: 63. when do i need to start ge
title: when do i need to start getting my breasts checked?
body:
24 y/o F. 4’11” 98 lbs no health concerns. 

Every time I go to the gyno she asks if I want a breast check. I always say no because I figured she’d wouldn’t give me the option if I needed it now. Is this the thing where they squish your breasts between plates?! When do I have to start saying yes?!

real_comments.comment: You never have to start saying yes. The doctor can't force you to get any tests, take any medications or undergo any exams. It's all your choice. You can ask at your next appointment what she recommends and then you can decide whether or not you want to follow her recommendations. I'm not sure where you're located and you haven't provided any information about your medical history or family history, so I can't comment on the general guidelines that would apply to you. In my area, people start getting yearly mammograms at age 45 if they have an average breast cancer risk. In my area, our public health authority doesn't have any firm guidelines for clinical breast exams.

The current recommendation is that you stay aware of your breasts and go to the doctor if you notice any changes in them. This is called “breast self-awareness”.

At a gyn appointment you can get an exam where a doctor feels for lumps, but you don’t need a mammogram yet. There is conflicting evidence about how useful these exams are, but many doctors will offer them.

Self breast exams are no longer recommended, as breast self awareness works better and resulted in fewer useless surgeries.

Somewhere between 40-50 years old most women will start to get mammograms, which is where your breasts are squished and an xray is taken of them to look for cancer.
My wife's breast cancer was detected by her gynecologist's physical examination. Consider agreeing.

DG.comment: The thing where they squish your breasts between plates is a mammogram, which is a type of x-ray. What your gynecologist is offering is a clinical breast exam, where she just uses her hands to feel for any lumps or abnormalities.
It's a good idea to start getting clinical breast exams in your 20s. It's a quick and simple part of a preventative health check-up.
She likely gives you the option to respect your autonomy, but it is a recommended screening for women your age. It helps to establish a baseline for what is normal for you.

In addition to the exam your doctor does, this is also a great age to become familiar with doing your own self-exams at home once a month. The goal is just to know what your tissue normally feels like.

SAG.comment: The breast check your gynecologist is offering is a manual exam where she feels for any lumps, not the mammogram you're thinking of with the plates. It's a good idea to let her do it as part of your routine physical.

The exam your doctor is offering is a clinical breast exam, where she would just feel for any lumps or abnormalities with her hands. The 'squishing between plates' you're thinking of is a mammogram, which is a type of imaging usually not recommended until you're older, unless you have specific risk factors.
The breast check your GYN is offering is a manual exam, not the mammogram (the 'squishing' machine). It's a good habit to get into so your provider can get a baseline of what's normal for you.

What your gynecologist is offering is a clinical breast exam, which is just a physical check for lumps, not a mammogram (the 'squishing' procedure). It's a good idea to start getting them so you know what is normal for you.

SAGII.comment: The check she's offering is a clinical breast exam where she just feels for any lumps. The 'squishing between plates' is a mammogram, which is a different screening test typically started at a later age.

Guidelines on routine clinical breast exams for your age group can vary, but it's a good way to establish a baseline for what's normal for you. It's also a good time to learn how to do a proper self-exam.

It's offered as an option because the recommendations for routine clinical breast exams in your age group have changed over the years. It's a simple manual exam, and doing it helps establish a baseline for what's normal for your body.

The manual exam is very quick and not uncomfortable. Your provider is simply feeling the tissue throughout the breast and under the arm to get a sense of what your normal is. It's helpful for tracking any potential changes over time.

title: X-ray may show uterine fibroid?
body: Hello all, I am a 27F and went to the chiropractor for help with my lower back pain. They did a pelvic X-ray and realigned my hips and I’m actually feeling a lot better. Problem is I’m looking at the X-ray image and trying to figure out if this lumpy glob on the right side is something to be worried about or a gas bubble. I’m worried it looks like a fibroid or could be cancer. Please have a look and let me know if you think I should ask for more tests from my regular doctor? (Image in the comments)

real_comments.comment: Those are farts. Stop going to chiropractors.

DG.comment: X-rays are for looking at bones, not soft tissues like the uterus. What you're seeing is almost certainly overlying bowel gas or stool which is completely normal.
If you are concerned about fibroids due to symptoms like heavy bleeding or pelvic pressure, the best test to get is a pelvic ultrasound. An x-ray is not the appropriate imaging for that.

SAG.comment: It's very common to see overlying bowel gas and stool on a pelvic x-ray, which can create all sorts of confusing shadows. That would be the most likely explanation for what you're seeing.
It's very difficult to differentiate soft tissue structures from overlying bowel gas or stool on a plain X-ray. This is not the right type of imaging to evaluate for something like a fibroid.

SAGII.comment: That's almost certainly stool and gas in your colon, which is overlying the area you're concerned about. X-rays are not the appropriate imaging modality to evaluate for things like uterine fibroids.
I would be very cautious about having a chiropractor interpret medical imaging; they are not radiologists. As the other commenter noted, this is a classic appearance of stool and gas in the colon.

title: Urologist suggested lithotripsy without another CT scan or anything to confirm if my kidney stone passed, thoughts??
body:
Age: 33

Sex: female

Height: 5’6

Weight: 240

Race: white

Duration of complaint: 14 days

Location: NY

Any existing relevant medical issues: PCOS + overweight

Current medications: none

On January 9 I began having severe pain in my right lower back and vomiting and slightly elevated temperature (99.4). Long story short went to ER, had blood and urine samples taken, transvaginal ultrasound and CT scan, ultimately was diagnosed with 6mm kidney stone in mid ureter and hydronephrosis of right kidney. Was given cephalexin, flowmax, and 600 mg ibuprofen prescriptions and was told it would likely pass on its own soon. Began taking meds as prescribed and had much less pain but still have some here and there. On a scale of 1-10 it’s usually a 1-2. Passed big clots whenever I would urinate and did not observe anything that resembled a kidney stone (hospital didn’t even give me a strainer!)

Saw urologist on 1/21 who informed me that I have additional stones in my right kidney (according to records from the hospital; he did NOT do any additional testing at my appointment) and suggested a lithotripsy with a stent procedure next week. He told me 6mm are difficult to pass on their own with 50% success rate. He did not seem concerned that I was passing clots when urinating.

Does it seem concerning that he kind of rushed to schedule me for a procedure without doing any additional CT scans or other testing? I did tell him that I didn’t see or feel like I passed anything besides the clots (I guess it’s possible it could have passed with a clot). Also told me I am too overweight to have a successful ESWL. I’m nervous about needing a stent I’ve heard they’re awful. 

Am I overthinking this? Should I see another urologist for a second opinion? I think the procedure is worth it to handle the other stones in my kidney but I’m just feeling kinda nervous and stressed out

real_comments.comment: Im not sure what additional testing is needed when we know you have stones

DG.comment: It's standard practice to get a repeat imaging study, like a KUB x-ray or a low-dose CT, before a procedure to confirm the stone is still there and see its current location. Especially since your symptoms have improved, it's very possible the stone has moved further down or even passed.

SAG.comment: It's standard practice to get a KUB x-ray on the day of the procedure to confirm the stone hasn't passed and to localize it for the surgery. I would ask your urologist if this is part of the plan.

SAGII.comment: This sounds like a very reasonable plan. For a 6mm stone that is still causing symptoms after two weeks, intervention is often the next step. A repeat CT isn't always needed, as they will use imaging during the procedure itself to find and treat the stone.

title: Please Help! How to avoid infection with open wound?
body:
22 (soon 23) Female

5'1

146 lbs

Medical Issues: GERD, Anxiety, Adenomyosis

Vape only

I had an external cyst removed down there (on the lip), and I just got my period. It’s been about a week and the wound hasn’t healed or anything(it’s a completely open wound no stitch). It’s literally fresh as if I got it today(the wound). I wear pads and i’m worried that the period blood will touch it and infect it. Please help! What should I do?!

real_comments.comment: Clean it with soap and water. Keep the area clean and dry during the day. Can apply a small amount of Vaseline to the opening if your want. Avoid submerging until healed.

DG.comment: You can gently rinse the area with warm water a few times a day, especially after changing your pad. Pat it dry very carefully with a clean cloth. Frequent pad changes will also help keep the area as clean as possible.
Keep an eye out for signs of infection like increased redness, warmth, foul-smelling drainage, or worsening pain. A wound that shows no signs of healing after a week is worth monitoring closely.

SAG.comment: Keep the area as clean and dry as possible. You can do gentle rinses with warm water (a peri bottle works well) and pat dry after using the restroom or changing your pad. Applying a thin layer of petroleum jelly can also help protect the wound.

You'll want to keep the area as clean and dry as possible. Gently rinse with warm water and pat dry every time you change your pad. Since it's been a week with no signs of healing, you should give your doctor's office a call to have it checked.

SAGII.comment: Gently rinse the area with warm water a few times a day and pat it dry. A peri bottle (squirt bottle) can make this easier. Be sure to change your pad very frequently to keep the wound as clean as possible.

Using tampons instead of pads would be a good way to keep the area as dry as possible. You could also apply a very thin layer of something like Vaseline over the wound itself to act as a barrier against moisture.

title: 22F inner thighs darkening

real_comments.comment:

title: Been in the hospital for 5 days with no answer
body:
Hello Reddit! I'm a 29 y/o female, 5'0" 120lbs. I am relatively healthy (eat decently well, prioritizing fruit, veg, and proteins but i still have treats) and workout about 2-3 times a week (weightlifting, biking, and bjj). I have hypothyroidism and I have been treating it since I was 21, and I only take 88 mcg. 

TLDR: been stuck in the hospital for 5 days, no diagnosis. what's my best course of action?  


Two weeks ago, I was on my period and experiencing diarrhea. I blamed my period for the diarrhea, but as time moved on, the diarrhea only got worse and the period went away. The diarrhea began to be entirely watery with blood mixed in. A decent amount of blood, not like a burst hemorrhoid, but like internal bleeding amount of blood. This started around 11/7. I would get intense bouts of nausea and then go to the bathroom. Usually after going to the bathroom, the nausea would go away. I haven't vomited once, but I'm still dealing with debilitating nausea.   
The bloody, watery stools continued all of last week. I tried to work through it, but it was hard. Finally, I went to urgent care Thursday night. They sent me to the ER.  
At the ER, they gave me fluids and sent me for a CT scan, which came back with a severely inflamed colon. The ER doctor referred to it as EXTENSIVE colitis. They admitted me after that and put me on courses of antibiotics (ciprofloxacin and metronadazole (sp?)) and fluids. When they admitted me, they told me it was because I needed immediate care and could not get it over the weekend if they sent me home.

Now it is Tuesday, and I have no diagnosis. I've given plenty of stool samples, blood, and been given CT scans, but no one has an answer. They say that they use an external lab, and the labs are really backed up which is why they've kept me for 5 days. They kept saying they would likely do a colonoscopy, but no one began prep for it, and every time I asked about it, they kept saying "in the next couple days." I've been kept in an isolated room because they were worried I have something infectious. The food here is beyond abysmal, so I don't understand how they expect me to heal my gut with this.

I believe this hospital is keeping me because I have insurance that pays them. It's a small, public hospital in NYC and their patient-base is not the wealthiest. Today, I woke up and told them that I would like to be transferred to a larger, private hospital, and no one has gotten back to me since. I cant walk out into the hallway because I'm in isolation and I don't know the rules. 

What's my best course of action? I asked for a transfer around 10am and I've been sitting here for two hours without anything. What do you recommend?

real_comments.comment:
This doesnt sound abnormal to me. 

You have got a diagnosis; colitis. We don't always find out what's caused it. 

The fact you are still being isolated means your stool sample results aren't back. Once they are back it will rule out/in infective causes like C-Diff and other bugs. 

Where I work, we generally like the acute episode of colitis (inflammation) to calm down before we do colonoscopies. Its common for us to send people home once the diarrhea and pain is manageable and bring them back for a colonoscopy to see if there's anything going on in the bowel. Those that do get them as inpatient are often waiting a few days.

DG.comment: Ask to speak to the case manager and the charge nurse on your floor regarding the transfer. They are the ones who facilitate this. You can also ask for the name of the attending hospitalist physician currently managing your care and request to speak with them directly about your plan and the transfer.

SAG.comment: With extensive colitis on CT and bloody diarrhea in your age group, they are likely working to differentiate between an infectious cause and a new onset of inflammatory bowel disease (like ulcerative colitis). The stool studies are key to figuring that out before they proceed with a scope.

SAGII.comment: It's standard practice to wait for infectious stool studies to come back negative before scoping, especially with severe colitis, to reduce the risk of perforation. Frustrating, but the lab delay is likely the main holdup.

title: [Acne] Recurring Cyst in the Same Spot on My Face. What Can I Do?
body:
I (Early 20s M) suddenly got a cyst on my cheek around a year and a half ago. It grew and after two weeks or so and applying warm compress it drained and the skin went back to looking normal. Since then I have had the same cyst return in the same spot 3 more times and the last time it drained after a week but the area remained red until it came back now. 

The cyst is oval-ish shaped and I'd estimate peaks around 3.5 cm in length, 2.5-3 cm in width, and 1 cm or so outwards. Its highly visible when its there since its red and inflamed and honestly it destroys my face and I don't even want to leave the house when it happens. 

I went to a doctor today since it just started coming back and she prescribed me a topical anti-biotic and some topical cortisone derivative as a steroid to fight the inflammation but prescribed it for 2 weeks which doesn't make sense it went away in a week last time. I'm not sure if this will be useful or if I should just wait for it to drain naturally. 

She also gave me a referral to a specialist to see if I would need some kind of removal procedure which honestly scares the hell out of me. I'm worried about scarring or something going wrong. 

What are the odds that its something that doesn't require a surgical procedure to remove? Maybe hormonal or some kind of clogged pore or something. Anyone have any experience with this? It truly is making me depressed and miserable because it feels uncomfortable and looks terrible.  
  
Any advice is appreciated.

real_comments.comment: Surgical excision is likely to be curative, or you can choose to keep it long-term.

DG.comment: A cyst that keeps coming back in the exact same spot often has a small sac under the skin that refills. Seeing the specialist is a good idea, as they can discuss options like injecting it with a steroid to shrink it or fully removing the sac to prevent it from returning.

SAG.comment: A cyst that keeps coming back in the same spot usually means there's an underlying sac that keeps refilling. Seeing the specialist for removal is the best way to get rid of it for good. It's a very common and minor procedure.

SAGII.comment: This sounds more like an epidermoid cyst than a typical acne cyst, given the recurrence in the same spot. The specialist referral is appropriate, as excision is the definitive treatment to prevent it from coming back.

title: 16 weeks pregnant — black liquid coming from my bum?
body:
(27F) I’m currently 16 weeks pregnant and just wanted to ask if anyone’s ever gone through something like this.

So earlier today, I was trying to poop because I’ve been constipated for a few days. The stool was really hard and wouldn’t come out no matter how much I tried (I didn’t force it too much though). Then I noticed this black liquid coming out of my butt instead. It kinda had a grainy texture too.

I freaked out, honestly. I called my OB right away, and she told me it’s most likely because of my iron supplements that they can cause black stool or discharge like that, as long as it’s coming from my rectum and not my vagina. She said not to worry, but just avoid straining too much.

Right now I’m still super constipated and it’s really uncomfortable. There’s still some black liquid coming out but no actual poop yet. I just wanted to ask — should I be asking for a second opinion just to be safe?

Please be kind, I’m a bit anxious and honestly just want to make sure my baby’s okay. 🥺

real_comments.comment: my thoughts are that it sounds like it could be overflow diahorrea which can be seen with constipation. it happens because watery stool can seep past the blockage.

DG.comment: Your OB's advice sounds spot on. Iron supplements are notorious for turning stool black, and the liquid consistency is likely mucus from the constipation and straining. You could ask your OB about taking a stool softener like docusate sodium (Colace) to help things along.

Black stool is the classic sign of taking iron supplements, so that part is not concerning. For the constipation, try to increase your water intake significantly and add more fiber to your diet. Polyethylene glycol (Miralax) is also generally considered safe and effective during pregnancy for constipation.

SAG.comment: Your OB is right, this is a very common side effect of iron supplements. The liquid you're seeing is likely stool and mucus that is able to get around the hard, impacted stool. Focusing on the constipation is your best bet; increasing water and fiber intake can help a lot.

The black color is almost certainly from your iron supplements, as your OB mentioned. For the constipation, focus on increasing your fluid and fiber intake. You can also ask your OB about starting a stool softener like docusate (Colace).

SAGII.comment: Your OB is correct; this is a very common side effect of iron supplements, especially when combined with constipation. The black liquid is likely looser stool seeping around a hard impaction. Try a stool softener like docusate sodium and increase your water intake.

Your OB's assessment is sound. For the constipation itself, you could try adding a daily dose of Miralax (polyethylene glycol) which is safe in pregnancy. Also, increasing dietary fiber with things like prunes or psyllium husk can be very helpful.

DG.comment: The 6-hour observation period is standard for this type of ingestion. Significant effects from oxymetazoline typically manifest well within that window, so it's a very reassuring sign that he was completely fine.

Yes, that's correct. The most concerning potential side effects like drowsiness, slowed heart rate, or breathing changes would have appeared during his observation at the hospital. The fact that he was discharged acting normally is an excellent sign.

SAG.comment: Yes, that's generally true. A 6-hour observation period where he was asymptomatic is very reassuring, as we would expect to see any significant adverse effects well within that timeframe.

Yes, that's correct. A 6-hour observation period is typically sufficient to see any potential adverse effects from that medication. The fact that he was completely asymptomatic during that time is a very good sign.

SAGII.comment: A six-hour observation period is standard for this type of ingestion. If he was completely asymptomatic during that time, it's very unlikely any new, serious symptoms would develop now.
The active ingredient in that spray acts fairly quickly. The fact that he was observed for 6 hours without any changes in his heart rate, breathing, or alertness is very reassuring.

title: 23M – Doctor recommends ciprofloxacin for pseudomonas folliculitis, but I’m scared of the side effects. Is it really the only safe option?

• HOCl spray
• topical sulfur
• acetic acid 0.5–1%
• mandelic/azelaic acid

SAG.comment: Ciprofloxacin is a reasonable choice given the confirmed sensitivity and failure of multiple other treatments. A short course is generally well-tolerated.

SAGII.comment: Given the sensitivities and the failure of multiple other treatments, ciprofloxacin is a very reasonable choice here. The risk of serious side effects with a short 10-day course is low, and this is a difficult infection to clear otherwise.

title: Unsure what kind of doctor to see? Getting off dual-purpose antiepileptic drug. Psychiatrist? Neurologist?
body:
24F

100lb

5’2

MEDS:

wellbutrin 300mg

lamotrigine 250mg

  
timeline:

2020: put on Wellbutrin and Lamictal for psych

2021: relapsed on drugs (PCP analogues, opiates, some benzodiazepines). began to experience involuntary muscle jerks.

2023: had my first and only seizure (tonic-clonic) that I know of. witnessed. 40 seconds, no awareness, came to in the ER confused and with a bitten tongue and shoulder pain. Negative CT. Discharged. clear EEG months later while on keppra as well.

haven’t worried about it since bc I’m now off drugs and still on lamotrigine. however, I now want to get off it due to side effects. been mostly stable psych-wise, no other seizures. 

my primary goal is assessing the seizure risk for discontinuing lamictal but remaining on wellbutrin. the other thing that makes me scratch my head is that I continue to experience involuntary muscle jerks. heard that can be a side effect of meds tho.

real_comments.comment:
It appears your seizure was provoked -- likely as a result of withdrawing from a substance.  

Because you had a single provoked seizure, Wellbutrin is typically continued.  

In this situation I'd see my psychiatrist about stopping Lamictal, because the Lamictal, in the scenario isn't a "dual purpose medicine" (you don't have a seizure disorder), it is a psychiatric medication, which just happens to also be labeled (indicated) for epilepsy. 

Involuntary muscle jerks -- most likely a lingering result of the PCP analogues.

DG.comment: A neurologist is the right specialist to discuss tapering an antiepileptic drug and to assess your overall seizure risk. It would be ideal for them to coordinate the taper with your psychiatrist, who manages your Wellbutrin.

SAG.comment: This is a situation where it would be best for both your psychiatrist and a neurologist to coordinate care. Given the history of a seizure and the use of Wellbutrin, a neurologist should be involved in assessing your seizure risk and creating a safe tapering plan for the lamotrigine.

SAGII.comment: A neurologist would be the most appropriate person to discuss this with. Tapering an anticonvulsant while on bupropion requires careful management due to seizure risk.

title: Why does my temperature drop instead of rise when I'm sick?
body:
I'm 17 AFAB and currently have COVID, which is what made me think of this and think to ask someone. For reference, my baseline temperature is 98.2°.

For at least the last year (can't remember how long it's been, it hasn't always been like this though) whenever I've gotten sick and it seems/feels like I should have a fever I'll check my temp and instead of been 99° or 100° like I'd expect I'm almost always down to 96.2-96.8°. It feels the same as when I have an actual fever, which is what confuses me. Like it's to the point that I have to check my temperature multiple different times with the different thermometers we have because I just can't believe that I'm not running a fever. I mentioned that I currently have COVID, but something interesting that happened was when I first got sick I had the low body temperature, then I felt better for a day and then the day that I started feeling worse I had an actual fever then it went back to low temperature.

I've checked it with different thermometers (as in several different oral and several different forehead ones) including ones at the doctors office/hospital so it's not just an error in the thermometer. Also taking Tylenol/Ibuprofen is rare for me so it's not that doing it either. I've been sick since Monday (it's Saturday now) and I just took ibuprofen for the first time because my throat hurts too much to sleep.

Does anyone have an explanation for this?

real_comments.comment: basically your body’s “set point” isn’t pushing heat, it’s conserving energy. super common in viral infections/fatigue states/smaller body frames. hypothalamus is reacting differently to the same cytokines. totally fine as long as you’re not dropping below ~95 or getting confused/shaky.

DG.comment: A low temperature can actually be another way the body responds to infection, though it's less common than a fever. The feeling of having a fever, like chills and aches, comes from your body's thermostat being reset by the immune response, which can happen even if your temperature drops instead of rises.

SAG.comment: This can be part of the systemic inflammatory response to an infection. The body is still mounting a defense, just with a different thermoregulatory response than the classic fever.

SAGII.comment: While a fever is the classic response, a drop in temperature can also happen during an infection. The subjective feeling of being feverish (chills, feeling hot/cold) is due to your body's thermostat being reset by the immune response, regardless of whether the final temperature goes up or down.

When they first started they were central chest pains which felt like a crushing feeling. I went to the er a few times with this, the pain would last all day for 2 weeks straight at times. My gp referred me to a cardiologist who did a CT scan, X-ray, bloods, ecg and a 24h ecg all of them were clear and I was told my pains were anxiety 

Those would continue for 2 years but then over the last year the pain shifted, it’s now on the left side, it’s still slightly central but now it’s also above and below the left nipple area, under the left armpit and spreads down that side, also sometimes in my upper left arm. This pain now is more of an ache pain rather than a crushing feeling. This pain can also last 1 day to 3 weeks all day everyday constant pain 

I’ve been to the er many times with this also because the pain gets severe, X-rays, ecgs & bloods done again all clear they said it’s anxiety or muscular pain. I spoke to my gp last week as Im again experiencing it bad and they said it could just be one of those things where nothing could be done.. they did refer me to pain management and right now that seems to be my last hope. They said a heart attack in a 28 year old is very very unlikely but my mind can’t shift that feeling when I’m experiencing this daily 

I do also get reflux which I’m on meds for but I’ve never had tests other than a h pylori test.

I’m wondering if I should give up? Do I have to suffer with this forever?

real_comments.comment: Pain like this can be due to acid reflux. How well controlled is it?

DG.comment: The pattern and location you're describing now (left side, under the armpit, ache) are very characteristic of musculoskeletal pain. It would be worth exploring a diagnosis of costochondritis, as it can cause severe, persistent chest wall pain.

Don't discount the reflux. It can cause significant chest pain that mimics a heart attack. Since the pain has changed and you haven't had a full workup for it, it may be worth asking your doctor about further GI investigation like an endoscopy.

SAG.comment: With a negative cardiac workup, it's reasonable to look at other causes. Have you considered a more thorough evaluation of your reflux, such as an endoscopy? Esophagitis can cause significant and persistent chest pain that mimics heart issues.

With a repeatedly negative cardiac workup and a history of reflux, it's worth exploring esophageal causes more thoroughly. Esophageal spasms or severe esophagitis can mimic cardiac pain and might not show up on the tests you've had.

SAGII.comment: The fact that you have reflux is a very important clue. Esophageal issues can cause severe and persistent chest pain that can be difficult to distinguish from cardiac pain. It may be worthwhile to discuss a more thorough GI workup with your GP.

That's a frustrating thing to hear from your doctor. The change in the character and location of your pain does make a cardiac cause much less likely. Seeing pain management is a good next step; they're specialists in figuring out these types of complex, non-cardiac chest wall pain syndromes.

sheet_name: 95. How exactly do they come t
title: How exactly do they come to a preeclampsia diagnosis when there's no symptoms?
body:
28F

6 weeks pregnant 

First baby born was via emergency c section at 33+3. I was admitted to the hospital at 33 for preeclampsia even though I didn't have any symptoms. I was at a routine prenatal appointment, not seeking care for any ailment. My blood work was fine. I didn't have headaches. Per Google, the standard for preeclampsia is 140/90. I stayed around 131/75 most of the time without medicine. The highest my BP got was 151/89 in the hospital and that appears to be only slightly elevated.

Now I'm considered a high risk pregnancy because I had preeclampsia but it doesn't even make sense to me why they gave me that diagnosis. I never saw starbursts. There was no blood or protein in my urine. I was neurologically intact. 

The emergency c section was due to decelerated heart rate cause by a double nuchal, so it wasn't event related to the blood pressure.

I am annoyed that they they kept me on bed rest and are going to treat me like I'm fragile this pregnancy. Not that it matters now, but I'm pretty sure baby and I would have been better off if I was allowed to be home. 

So how do doctors actually make the call for a preeclampsia diagnosis?

real_comments.comment:
If they diagnosed you with preeclampsia, you met criteria for preeclampsia somehow. Diagnosis is not necessarily dependent on symptoms, though symptoms can be included in diagnosis.

You state your highest blood pressure was 151/89, which would meet criteria for at least gestational hypertension, and all you would have needed is one other systolic >140 or diastolic >90 after 20 weeks gestation to meet that criteria for preeclampsia. If at any point you had proteinuria as measured in one of several methods (not just straight protein), low platelets, elevated LFTs, elevated creatinine, headache not accounted for by other causes, pulmonary edema, or visual symptoms you would meet criteria for preeclampsia.

Your OB team found you met another diagnostic criteria somewhere along the way. The treatments and recommendations surrounding preeclampsia are to reduce risks to both you and baby, regardless of presence of symptoms. It also sounds like they were also watching for a fetal anomaly and admitted you for monitoring of that condition as well.

Also, you had an emergency C-section due to non-reassuring fetal heart rate at 33+3 and you feel like you would have been better off at home? If your baby was already showing signs of fetal distress, it’s more likely there could have been a catastrophic outcome had you not been monitored, since those decelerations would still have occurred but you would never have known until it was too late.

Right now, it sounds like you are worried about what they are going to do before they’ve even made any recommendations. Take it one step at a time and discuss your concerns with your doctor.

DG.comment: The diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia no longer strictly require protein in the urine. A diagnosis can be made based on new-onset high blood pressure along with other findings, like changes in your platelet count or liver function tests, even if you don't have any symptoms.

SAG.comment: While your blood pressure readings might not have seemed very high to you, the diagnosis can be based on new-onset hypertension plus other specific lab findings. They may have seen something concerning with your platelet count or liver function tests that warranted the diagnosis, even without protein in your urine.

SAGII.comment: The diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia have evolved. A diagnosis can be made based on elevated blood pressure plus other findings like low platelets or elevated liver enzymes, even in the absence of protein in the urine or other symptoms.

title: Did I hallucinate? Worried about rabies
body:
22F! 

I’m so scared and worried I’m having rabies symptoms, a few days ago I threw up and after that, I seemed to be fine. Now I’m having tingling and I think I hallucinated today.

I was watching a show with my friends today and I thought I saw a face appear in one of the scenes, I looked back and didn’t see it again and freaked out because hallucinations are a sign of rabies. I don’t know what to do. I don’t want to die.

I haven’t seen a bat around or in my house but I’m worried somehow one got in the attic and went through the vent, into my room or the house and bit me.

real_comments.comment:
You should be worried about rabies if you had contact with an animal that has rabies. You have had no contact with the a bat. If there was a bat in your house I would say it would be reasonable to get checked out, but hallucinations are far more likely to be a sign of psychosis than a sign of rabies, especially when there’s been no evidence *at all* of contact with a rabid animal. 

Yes you need to see a doctor, but that doctor should be a psychiatrist
If you truly have symptoms of rabies, the best thing to do is get your affairs in order.

DG.comment: Seeing something for a split second in a TV show that isn't there when you look again isn't a hallucination in the clinical sense. It's an extremely common trick of the eye, often related to hypervigilance.
Tingling sensations are a classic physical symptom of anxiety. When your fight-or-flight system is activated from stress, it can cause all sorts of strange feelings like that.

For rabies to be a concern, there generally needs to be a known or highly probable exposure to an infected animal, like a bite or scratch. A hypothetical scenario without any evidence of a bat is not a typical risk factor.
A single episode of vomiting a few days ago is very nonspecific and unlikely to be related to the tingling you're experiencing now. It could have been caused by countless things.
The way you describe your symptoms—a few different, vague physical feelings combined with an intense fear of a specific, rare disease—is very characteristic of severe health anxiety.
It sounds like this fear is causing you significant distress. Speaking with a primary care provider or a therapist about these anxieties can be very helpful for getting them under control.

SAG.comment: The combination of GI upset followed by tingling and a feeling of heightened awareness is very characteristic of a somatic response to anxiety. It's much less indicative of an infectious process like rabies, especially without a known exposure.

Seeing a face in a busy scene that isn't there when you look back is a very common trick of the eye, not a hallucination. Anxiety can definitely make you more hyper-aware of these normal perceptual glitches.

Significant anxiety can cause a wide range of physical symptoms, including nausea and tingling sensations. It can also make you hypervigilant, which might explain why you're noticing things you otherwise wouldn't.

Seeing a fleeting image or face on a screen isn't usually considered a hallucination in the clinical sense. It's a common perceptual trick your brain can play, especially when you're feeling stressed or hyper-aware.

Intense anxiety can cause a wide range of physical symptoms, including tingling sensations. It can also make you hyper-aware of your surroundings, which could explain misinterpreting something you saw briefly.

What you describe sounds much more consistent with a high level of anxiety than rabies. Tingling and misperceiving something briefly on a screen are classic signs of your nervous system being on high alert from stress.

SAGII.comment: Seeing something for a split second that isn't there when you look back is a very common trick of the eye and brain. It's not typically considered a hallucination in the clinical sense, especially when you're feeling stressed or anxious.

It sounds like you're incredibly anxious, and that level of stress can absolutely cause physical symptoms like tingling and stomach upset. Your brain is on high alert, which can also make you more likely to misinterpret things you see or hear.
The proposed exposure scenario for rabies is extremely improbable. Your symptoms, including the tingling and what you perceived as a hallucination, are very common manifestations of severe anxiety.

The neurologic symptoms of rabies are very specific and severe, such as having spasms when trying to drink water or when feeling a breeze on your skin. What you're describing is much more consistent with the physical effects of high anxiety.

This specific fear about rabies from a potential unwitnessed bat exposure is an incredibly common theme for people struggling with health anxiety. The symptoms you're describing are also textbook examples of how severe anxiety can manifest physically.

Once the neurological symptoms of rabies begin, it is a very rapid and severe illness, not something that comes and goes. The tingling you're experiencing is a very non-specific symptom that can have many causes, with anxiety being a very common one.

title: Is it ok to just monitor my mole for now? (Image in comments)
body:
25M, 5"9, 150lbs




I am not sure when exactly I first got this mole because it is on my back so I can’t easily see it, but I know I’ve had it for at least 2.5 years because a dermatologist from before I moved mentioned it. They said that it was a very dark mole, but didn’t make a big deal out of it and in general I should just be on the look out if a mole is growing/changing. Their medical notes described the mole as a dark, evenly pigmented 4mm nevus.







I didn’t see a dermatologist and didn’t keep track of it since, until a few months ago when I went to a new dermatologist and he noticed the same mole. He said that the mole was black/darker than all my other moles and said I should have it excised just in case. I didn’t think I could afford a full excision so I just chose to monitor it for these past few months. I’ve started taking photos and measuring it monthly, and the recent photos match the description from 2.5 years ago that the other dermatologist had given of a dark, evenly pigmented 4mm nevus.







A couple of months from the initial visit I saw him again and he said that it looked the same size, and that he thinks it is probably benign, but he would still recommend having it biopsied since he likes to be extra careful and because it was different than the rest of my moles, or he said I could come in every 6 months to check if it is changing/growing. I asked him what type of biopsy and he said it would be a shave biopsy (I’m not sure if he always meant to do shave biopsy, or if he initially offered a full excision during my first appointment and is now changing his mind?)







I have heard some stories of people who have had their mole regrow after a shave biopsy, and I’ve also heard that for some people their mole regrew to be malignant despite their initial shave biopsy coming back as benign.







I think my mole is probably nothing serious and is probably benign, but I am not sure if I should do the shave biopsy because the shave wouldn’t completely remove the mole, so I am afraid that making mole’s surface not visible will make it harder to monitor the mole in the future.







I am thinking that since my mole is visible, if there are any changes I could immediately notice (and get a full excision if I could afford it). But if I do a shave biopsy then I can’t see the mole’s surface, so if it becomes malignant in the future it would spread deeper without me knowing and I won’t notice until later when the mole re-emerges to the surface.







Would it be alright to just monitor the mole for now?

real_comments.comment: The spot that you show is likely benign. Note that without examining all of your skin, it is difficult to know whether this is normal or fulfills the "ugly duckling sign." Moreover, most people who post on this site do not use high-resolution macro lenses or dermoscopic photography. If you are concerned, seek care.

DG.comment: A mole that looks different from all your others, often called an 'ugly duckling,' is typically one that dermatologists will have a lower threshold to biopsy. Even with a history of stability, the fact that it's an outlier often warrants a closer look pathologically.

SAG.comment: The recommendation to biopsy is likely based on the 'ugly duckling' sign, meaning it looks different than your other moles. Even if a lesion is stable, being an outlier is often enough reason to get a tissue diagnosis.

SAGII.comment: That's a classic 'ugly duckling' mole. Biopsying a lesion just because it looks different from all the others is a very standard and reasonable approach, even if it hasn't been changing.

title: Chronic Chest Pain for nearly a year (22F)
body:
I started experiencing pain in the centre of my chest around January this year, the pain has fluctuated over the months but never fully went away.


• Endoscopy found nothing.
• Blood tests normal.
• ECG normal.
• Awaiting cardiologist appointment.
• Pain is central, feels like pressure around the sternum, doesn't get better or worse with exertion but gets slightly worse when I bend down and forward. Pain can radiate into the left arm and left side of neck on occasion. The pain does not get worse when I press down on my chest.
• I sometimes also feel a fluttering/spasming sensation in the same area. It is not painful but can feel uncomfortable and be alarming.
• I have a history of bad anxiety and this pain came on after a bad panic attack but not sure if it's related.


I've been to the doctor several times this year complaining about this but they don't seem to want to take me seriously. This pain is seriously ruining my life. Any advice on any further tests I should do or what might be going on would really help.

real_comments.comment:
> I've been to the doctor several times this year complaining about this but they don't seem to want to take me seriously. 

Endoscopy, blood tests, ECG, cardiology referral? What would “taking you seriously” look like to you?

These are classic panic attack symptoms and it sounds like they have occurred immediately following those episodes. The cardiology appointment should definitively rule out a cardiac cause (extremely unlikely but not impossible), after which hopefully you can move on with your life. Anxiety is a beast! (Or another b-word…) Good luck with that appointment.

DG.comment: The fact that the pain gets worse when you bend forward could suggest a gastrointestinal cause like reflux or esophageal spasm, even with a normal endoscopy. The fluttering sensation can also be related to that.

It's very common for anxiety and panic disorders to cause real, physical chest pain and sensations like fluttering. It's great that you are seeing a cardiologist to complete the workup and rule out other causes.

SAG.comment: A normal endoscopy doesn't fully rule out esophageal issues like motility disorders or esophageal spasm, which can cause pressure and a fluttering sensation. The fact that it's worse when bending over could also be a clue in that direction.
Given your symptoms and normal initial workup, musculoskeletal causes or something like esophageal spasm could be possibilities. It's good you're following up with cardiology to be thorough.

SAGII.comment: It's good that you have a cardiology appointment scheduled. They will likely want to do an echocardiogram and possibly a Holter monitor to evaluate the fluttering sensation you're experiencing.
The fact that it gets worse when you bend forward is an interesting clue. That positional nature can sometimes point towards an esophageal or musculoskeletal cause, even with a normal endoscopy.
